THE TWO BOOKS ON VARIOUS ISSUES TO SIMPLY
INTRODUCTION

When the drama of the conversion of Saint Augustine was approaching its happy ending, a venerable monk intervened, resplendent with the grace of God: Simplician. His portrait has received a distinguished aura from mentioning it in the book of Confessions: "And you suggested to my spirit, and it seemed reasonable to me, the idea of going to Simplician, who proved to be your good servant and the grace of God shone in him. In addition to this, I had heard from him that from his youth he lived very devotedly for you. At that time he was already old and it seemed to me that due to his long age, consumed with such a good desire to follow your paths, I had accumulated much experience and carried much doctrine, and this was in fact true. That is why I wanted, in conference with him on the bitter tide of my perplexities, that, taking into account the current disposition of my spirit, he would declare to me what was the best way to walk your path. ennoble and grace the countenance of a human creature. The old monk stood like those mountains of God, reverberating with clarity, which are the homines magni, homines clari, of which the Saint speaks in one of his sermons 2. He was an enlightened man, who with the calm radiance of his certainties and examples could guide and comfort the pilgrims of the heavenly homeland. There has been no shortage of those who wanted to link this ermine and shining figure with saints, denying him the influence on Augustine's religious decision. In fact, Prospero Alfaric accuses the Saint of having exaggerated the part that the monk had in his return to faith, for panegyric purposes, since he had then occupied—(date of the writing of the Confessions—the see of Milan as successor of Saint Ambrose 8. The Milanese counselor did two great benefits to Saint Augustine: he illuminated the path of new life and brought to the cowardly and downcast heart the burning brand of the history of a contemporary convert, a professor of rhetoric like him. Augustine had very good times and interviews with the monk, who enjoyed esteem and reputation in the Church of Milan as an ascetic and intellectual. He had traveled widely throughout the world to be instructed in the faith and knowledge of divine truths, and day and night he devoted himself to the reading of holy books, showing a singular penetration into. intelligible things and the ability to criticize and show the falsehoods of the philosophers and philosophies of that time 4. The phrase of Saint Ambrose—acri praesertim. ingenio etiam intelligibilia- complectens—gives reason to believe that Simplician professed the Platonic doctrine about the intelligible world, which is perhaps the most glorious conquest and revelation of Hellenic genius and a point of connection and harmony with the dogmatic thought of Christianity. He knew Plato's thoughts from his readings and from the relationship and friendship he had with the translator and popularizer of some Neoplatonic works in the West, Mario Victorino, the best Latin rhetorician and orator of that time, awarded with a statue from the Forum in Rome. Agustín had precisely read those books, and the flame they raised still burned alive in his chest. Unlike other philosophical sects, with Plato's he had experienced a rapid rise in vital forces. That was a healthy leap from the shadows to the light. After so many gasps and hesitations, Platonism emerged in his eyes as a beacon of light in the stormy and prolix night. But he still felt the burden of passions, the pondus consuetudinis carnalis, and he hesitated about the kind of life he should undertake. And threading the conversation with the topic of his recent readings, known to both, the young man revealed to the old man with an exemplary life the state of his consciousness, the tremulous world of his desires, the failed struggles.

two by the conquest of the new ideal, the ambiguities and detours of his laborious pilgrimage—circuitus errorum—, the practical hesitations about the future, the discovery of the intelligible world with the method of withdrawal into himself, and as a consequence, the new expansion of his thought and life. Simpliciano deepened in him the favorable impression that the books of the Neoplatonists had made on him, rejoicing that he had read them, because in them there is, insinuated in a thousand ways, a certain initiation into God and into his Word: in istis mitem omnibus modis insinuate Deum et Verbum eiusr'. The relationship between Platonic philosophy and Christianity was then a current topic. A disciple of Flotinus, Afrnelius, had already tried to prove that the mystery of the Incarnation, venerated by Christians, was derived from Plato's speculation about the fall of souls into bodies. There were no shortage of those in Milan, obtuse and arrogant, who denied the originality of Christianity, propagating that Jesus had taken some doctrines from Plato's writings. Saint Ambrose came out against this error, refuting it with great copy of reasons e. The dialogues between Simplician and Augustine continued on these tasty topics of philosophical and current culture, the conversation sometimes falling on the magnificent prologue of the Gospel of Saint John and the doctrine of the Word of God. Augustine then picked up from the lips of his interlocutor the saying of a Platonist, which he has preserved for us in the City of God: "This prologue of the Gospel, which bears the name of Saint John, said a Platonic philosopher that it should appear written in letters of gold in the most visible places in all the churches, as we used to hear from the holy elder Simplician, who was later bishop of Milan." 7 But, above all, one of the most beautiful remains of those edifying conversations. golden legends that is-

They malt the book of Confessions: the story of Victorinus' conversion. Due to the vividness and colorful details with which it is written, it is seen that that unfading story still endures in the eyes of Saint Augustine like a fresh dawn, filled with the joy and melody of the nightingale. "From the moment your servant Simplician told me about the conversion of Victorinus, I was inflamed with the desire to imitate him: for this purpose he told it to me" 8. That story passed through his soul as a passionate African like a loving ember or like a burning coal. Exempla sunt carbones vastatoms, the Saint will later say, undoubtedly remembering the ancient burn of the example of the conversion of a professor of rhetoric, like him, who "was not ashamed to become a priest of Christ and bowed his neck to the yoke of humility and bowed his forehead to the shame of the cross." perplexities, because later I was an admirer of his books. And the approval of the teacher was no small relief for the African writer, to whom he replied around the year 397: "When what I write pleases you, I already know who it pleases, because I know who dwells in you. For the same distributor and author of all spiritual gifts will confirm my obedience with your opinion. All the delight that those writings of mine produce in you is due to the Lord, who, using me, has said: Let there be light; and When you approved it, God saw that everything was good." He asked Saint Ambrose to exegete some passages from his letters before the people. "You have told me that it would be very pleasing to you if I declared to the people some passages from the writings of Saint Paul, because of the barely comprehensible depth of his advice, the sublimity of his sentences, which elevate the spirit, and because of the ardor with which they inflame the inquirers of his thought" 12. r Omf'., VIII, 5. The same desire moved him to consult Saint Augustine about some difficult passages of the Epistle to the Romans. Particularly the fact of the reprobation of a large mass of the chosen people has always been a tempting secret for the curiosity of Christians and for many a source of scandal. The Apostle faces the mystery there and emerges through the powers of God's justice and mercy. Those passages have a close relationship with the question of grace and lead to the terrifying problem of predestination. There, in the figure of Jacob and Esau, one preferred and the other rejected, the gratuitousness of divine gifts is evident, the freedom of the Lord, from whom no one can take the palm of his generous initiatives. Regarding this doctrine, Saint Augustine reconciles some passages of Scripture and justifies divine conduct within a general plan of Providence, which knows how to assign its proper place to those it does not admit as diners of its eternal glory. Thus the Doctor of Grace revealed to us new nuances of his thought, and long before entering into the fray with the Pelagians, he formulated the principles of Catholic doctrine and the refutation of their heresy. "Simplician, successor of Saint Ambrose in the see of Milan, among other questions that he proposed to his former disciple, Augustine, questioned him about chapter 10 of the Epistle to the Romans. The answer given in De diversis quaestionibus ad Simplicianum constitutes for its precision, its fullness and clarity, and above all for the rational explanation that it adds to the dogma, the true key to the Augustinian system" T3. '"From the year 397—adds J. Martin—is the period of exact knowledge, and it can be said to be definitive." In fact, this treatise has two titles that particularly recommend it to the attention of historians of dogma. Of course, he marks a very important stage in the history of the development of Augustinian thought.

This stage is all the more important as its writing indicates a date prior to the birth of Pelagianism and has as a consequence coram populo ad disputandum assumerem, quod eius profundum in consiliis vix comprehendatur, sublime in sententiis audientem erigat, disputantem accendat (Epist. ad Simplicianum, XXXVII, 1: PL 13XVI, 1084). The expression revealed to me can be explained by the mysterious influence that God as absolute truth has on the course of ideas, according to the Saint: Ubique vertías praesides consentibus te. You are the truth and everywhere you are present to respond to those who consult you 1S. It may also have a stricter sense of particular revelation, as when we speak of those made to the saints, v. gr., the Revelations of Saint Bridget, because he was, says Saint Posidius, "the main member of the body of the Lord, always solicitous and alert to ensure the needs of the Catholic Church" in. Interpret the word debatable however you want, it is true that Saint Augustine, when writing his responses to Simplician, already offered a complete and masterful conception of the grace of God. With it, the "ingrates", the deniers of God's maximum benefit to man, were defeated in their last stronghold. As we will see, this book has had a universal resonance in the domains of the highest theological speculation on the concord of grace and free will, which makes true the words of a modern historian of the

dogmas: "Saint Augustine divulged so many truths of a natural and supernatural order, that all the schools of the West were born from its copious abundance, and the teachers of mysticism and scholastic theology were also fed by it; the theological and philosophical life of the Middle Ages sprang from it" 20. Also here the apostle Saint Paul guided him to the depths of the mystery of Christ, and Simplician gave him the impetus to do so, asking him to paraphrase chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Romans. I had already tried twice before to comment on the aforementioned letter. In the year 394 he wrote the Exposition of some propositions contained in the Epistle to the Romans 21. Being a simple priest, on a trip to Carthage, he read said letter together with other colleagues, and as there were many passages that were difficult to understand, many questions were proposed to him, to which he responded as best he could. His friends asked him to give them the explanation in writing, and he did so, publishing the booklet referred to here 22. But, as the Saint himself recognizes in his Retractions, he had not yet delved into the mystery of predestination and grace, and statements escaped him that were later corrected. He believed in the need for grace for works, not for faith. Man himself can have the desire to believe and adhere to the truth that is shown to him, just as the sick person can desire healing and health. The velle credere, baptizan, curan, sanan did not belong to the category of works under whose name those of mercy are particularly included. The main error of this first-time comment is contained in the following words: Non ergo elegit Deus bene operants, sed credentes potius ut Ipse illos faciat bene operants. Nostrum est enim credere et velle:. illius autem, I will give credentibus et volentibus facultatem bene operandi per Spiritum Sanctum, per quem caritas Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris, ut nos misericordes efficiat. God did not choose those who did good works, but rather those who already believed to grant them the power to do good works. It is up to us to believe and want; to Him, to give to those who believe and want the power to do good by virtue of the Holy Spirit, through whom divine charity has been poured into our hearts to move us to works of mercy 23.

The consultation of Saint Simplician forced Saint Augustine to return to the difficult argument, and in two books he sent him the solution to the proposed questions. In the first, the fragments of the Letter to the Romans (7, 7-27) that deal with fallen man under the law, grace and the problem of predestination are interpreted. "It is one of the most dramatic pages of the Epistle to the Romans," says a contemporary commentator 1. The Doctor of Grace warns us of falling into two abysses: on the one hand, that of the fatalistic and Manichean conception of the lame man opens up, who is a collision field of two antagonistic forces and distrusts of saving himself, because he is dominated by the dark and tyrannical power of the evil principle; On the other is the abyss of Pharisaic and Pelagian presumption, which trusts in the moral equipment of natural energies provided by the law to practice all justice. Against the Manichaeans and their pessimism of the law it was necessary to prove the harmony of the two Testaments, the legitimacy and convenience of the ancient economy; and against the latter, the insufficiency of the law and free will for the fulfillment of justice. In the exegesis of this chapter, Saint Augustine later modified his opinion about the subject of man who groans so painfully under the weight of the law. In the first comments he believed that chapter 7 describes the man overwhelmed by divine commandments before receiving grace: Homo d~scribitur sub lege positus ante gratiam2. He does not lack desires or rather whims to do good; but the will surrenders to the force of evil. In the year 395 he still wrote: Sunt vtrba hominis sub lege constituti, nondum, sub graphy, quia etiam si nolit peccare, vincitur a peccato.3 These are the words of the man who gasps under the law and is not in grace, since sin tyrannizes him, even though he desires not to sin. The same exegesis continues in this book that we translate here. The Apostle personifies or configures man under the law and speaks through his mouth. Much more important and famous is the commentary on chapter 9, 10-23, where it touches on the very serious questions related to predestination and Christian vocation. The Apostle, after having celebrated the triumphs of grace and the fruits of faith in Christ, is assailed by the vision of the chosen people, who, having been favored with the most distinguished privileges, were for the most part excluded from the inheritance of the Messiah. Those who first received the divine call to the kingdom of grace repudiated the heavenly message. How is this fact explained, or rather, how is it justified? The Apostle defends the conduct of God, appealing to the absolute freedom of the divine benefactor to make his gifts, and alleges some examples from the Old Testament in proof of his doctrine. Both mercy and justice are hidden from human eyes in the depths of the Creator's unfathomable counsels. The entire Epistle is an allegation against the Pelagians, since its argument deals with justification by faith and the insufficiency of the law or the Mosa'oa economy to sanctify men, so that no one may become conceited or boast about their merits. In the fragment analyzed by Saint Augustine, Saint Paul tries to prove the gratuitousness of Israel's privileges with the example of the election of Isaac and Jacob. The Apostle's mind does not go as far as that of his commentator, that is, to the depths of predestination, because the divine election, according to the former, falls on Jacob as progenitor of the chosen people, a privilege that God was not obliged to grant him. These passages are not even about the granting of grace, but about the transfer of the estate, made in favor of Jacob to the exclusion of Esau, without prior merits or demerits on both sides. Following the argument of the Epistle to the Romans, in which Saint Paul sought to quell all pharisaic vainglory of one's own merits, due to the fulfillment of the law, to the effort of free will, Saint Augustine presents in this book in a new light the divine pillar of salvation. In the year 394 he made the decree of salvation depend on the foresight of personal merits. Foreknowledge was the first divine act, which regulated the others, and it was also regulated by the merits of human initiative. In the year 397, delving into the passages of the Apostle, where the sovereignty of grace is so highlighted, he understood that predestination is the beginning and the first ring of divine benefits and an absolute decree, independent of all previous merit. Mercy goes ahead in all divine works and calls and inspires the will to believe and comes with a long hand to the aid of man: it helps to do good and gives the strength to persevere to the end, to later crown those who have fought legitimately. Grace, then, takes the lead over all merit: Ante omne meritum es gratia; Such is the axiom of this book, which will illuminate the process of human redemption and will dominate Catholic soteriology. i Where, then, are we to look for the remote origins or first initiative of salvation, whether it concerns individuals or the human community? It is necessary to rise to the depth of the thoughts and eternal counsel of God. To obtain the palm of happiness, two things are required: the desire to obtain it and the career of the justified man who does good. The first can be had by man for himself; the second must be received from God. Man can ask, desire, prepare, trust the doctor; but healing is due to the art of it. A purely external appeal is sufficient for justification. But in the book addressed to Simplician, the Augustinian vocation, high secret atque, is enriched with new elements and is invested by the force of God. In the depths of the spirit, the divine power is revealed to change men and make them docile to the voice of the Gospel. In this aspect, a disciple of Saint Augustine, Egidio Romano, defines the vocation well: Impulsus et motus divinus, sen, compunctiones et bonae cogitationes: haec est divina pulsatio et divina statio ad ostium cordis pulsans, et vocatio Dei2i. It is easy to notice in the divine Scripture two kinds of passages: some that celebrate the effects of the mercy and grace of God, which triumphs; others, according to which the divine call suffers a rejection by creatures, fading into the void. Saint Augustine agrees with these passages, distinguishing two kinds of vocation: the one in a certain way lacks proportion and appropriateness with the spirit and inclinations of those who are called; the other, on the contrary, makes a concordant agreement with the space of those who receive the call. In the latter case God knocks on the door of his creature, and she answers: "Here I am; thy will be done." He calls this congruent or effective vocation, a qualifier with which he wanted to penetrate a little into the mysterious secret of God's action, which adapts wonderfully to the particular nature of each person, and has given rise to various explanatory essays to investigate the ultimate reason.

Thus the Lord, when He makes vessels of condemnation from the mass of the wicked, does not hate what He does, that is, the ordering of punishment, justly punishing those who are lost and giving opportunity to save those whom He pities 33. In fact, grace and truth did not come through Jesus Christ, in order to fulfill the law, which Moses gave to inspire fear. If the law is good, why did the sinful inclinations, strengthened by the law, work in our members and bear fruit of death? By those sinful inclinations which have frequently been alluded to, he meant the increase of concupiscence and the risk of punishment on account of the transgression of the command; that is, that. Sin, abusing a good thing, brought death, so that the precept made the sinner or sin extremely guilty. If the law is good, why are we free from the law of death, which bound us, so that we serve God with a new spirit and not according to the old letter? Because the law is a letter for those who do not comply with it because of the spirit of love, which incorporates them into the New Testament. Thus, those who are dead to sin are free from the letter, which enslaves those who do not comply with the law as prisoners. Because the law is simply a letter for those who know how to read it, but cannot comply with it. Those for whom it was written know it; But since they only know it when it is written and read, not because they love it and fulfill it, it turns out that for them it is only a letter, which does not help the one who reads it, but rather accuses the transgressor. Those who receive the new spirit are freed from their punishment, so that they are no longer obliged to the letter, which threatens punishment, but live from their profound intelligence, because they love justice. Hence the saying: The letter kills, the spirit gives life. Because the law, when it is only read, but not understood or fulfilled, it is true that it kills, because then it is called a letter. But the Spirit gives life, because the fullness of the law is charity, which has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who was given to us.

And for this reason they did not want grace to be given to the Gentiles, as unworthy of it, if they did not first profess the Mosaic religion. This question, raised then, is resolved in the Acts of the Apostles. They did not understand that, because the Gospel is grace, it is not due to the merit of works, otherwise grace is not grace. This thought is repeated in many places, putting the grace of faith before works, not to annul these, but to show that they do not precede grace, but rather follow it, so that no one flatters himself that he has received grace for the good works he did, but knows that he could not do well if he had not received grace through faith. And man begins to receive grace from the moment he begins to believe in God, moved to embrace faith by an internal or external warning. But it is important to distinguish at what moments or by what celebration of mysteries divine grace is infused with more fullness and evidence. Well, the catechumens also believe, and let us say the same about Cornelius, when with his alms and prayers he became worthy of the sending of an angel; But he would not have acted like this if he had not believed before, nor would he have had faith in any way unless he had been called, either by some mysterious visions of the mind or spirit, or by other more manifest warnings, notified by the senses. But in some, the grace of faith is still not enough to obtain the kingdom of heaven, as in the catechumens and in Cornelius himself, before joining the Church through the reception of the sacraments; In others, however, it is so great that they are part of the body of Christ and have become the temple of God. For the temple of God is holy, says the Apostle, and so are you. And the Lord himself says: Unless a man is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven. There are, then, germinations of faith similar to conception; But to reach eternal life it is not enough to be conceived, it is also necessary to be born. In fact, no one could maintain that Jacob, even before being born, had merited by his works that the Lord preferred him, saying: And the older will serve the younger. Isaac was not only promised when he was told: At this time I will return and Sarah will have a son. And in truth, neither had he merited by any work that his birth was promised, so that in Isaac the offspring of Aibrahan would be called; That is to say, those who considered themselves children of the promise were to belong to the inheritance of the saints in Christ, without being conceited about their own merits, but attributing to the grace of the call the privilege of being co-heirs of Christ, since when the promise was made, in order for them to be so, those who did not exist had not yet deserved anything. But Rebekah also had them at the same time as our father Isaac. And with great warning he says that he had them from a single conception, because they were twins. He could not, therefore, attribute to the merits of the father, as if someone were to say such a thing: The son was born in this way because the father was affected in such a way at the moment of begetting them, or the mother was affected in such a way when she conceived them. With the same seminal act the former procreated them at the same time, and the latter conceived them simultaneously. Saint Paul pondered the simultaneous conception of both, to also remove all pretext from astrologers, or rather those called genethacos, who are dedicated to predicting the customs and lives of men based on the circumstances that accompany their births. But here they do not know how to explain the differences that are observed in the twins, having been conceived at the same time, under the same disposition of the sky and the stars, so that no diversity can be applied to each one, and they can easily understand, if they want, that the horoscopes that they sell to the unfortunate are not based on any art, but are casual conjectures. But, returning to our argument, the Apostle mentions these things with a view to breaking and abasing the pride of men who are ungrateful to the grace of God and who dare to gloat over their merits. For when they had not yet been born or done anything good or bad, not as a reward for their works, but by the will of the one who called, it was said to him: The elder will serve the younger. Therefore grace is to him who calls, and good works follow him who receives grace; They do not produce grace, but rather, they are the fruit of grace.

For the fire does not heat to burn, but because it burns; nor does the wheel run well so that it is round, but because it is round; In the same way no one does good to receive grace, but because he has received it. 9. Without a doubt the Apostle foresaw the difficulty that these words could raise in the minds of the listeners and readers and then added: What shall we say then? Is there injustice in God? No way. And to remove all iniquity from Him, He says: For He said to Moses: I have mercy on whom I have mercy, and compassion on whom I have compassion. But do these words unleash or add to the difficulty? Well, here is precisely the crux of the matter: if God has compassion on whom he has compassion, and works mercy on whomever he pleases, why did Esau lack this mercy, so that through it he could be good, as Jacob was good through it? Or perhaps the words: I have mercy on whom I have mercy, and compassion on whom I have compassion, mean that to those whom God has mercy to call, he will also have mercy to draw them to faith, and to those whom he compassionately draws to faith, he will give mercy, that is, he will show them mercy so that they do good? And this is a warning so that no one should boast and boast even about the works of mercy, as if by them, as his own thing, he had merited the favor of God; for even to practice the works of mercy he has received mercy from him who distributes it according to his good pleasure. And if anyone is proud of having deserved it for his faith, know that he also received the gift of believing from the one who manifests his mercy by inspiring faith, who, while still unfaithful, looked at him with compassion to call him. Purified from their ungodliness, they were converted, believing in him who justifies the wicked, because God hates ungodliness. Therefore, in some he punishes it by condemning them, in others he destroys it by justifying them, as he judges should be done in his impenetrable judgments. And although he makes the number of the wicked that he does not justify into vessels of ignominy, he does not hate their own making in them, because, as wicked, they are worthy of execration; but since they are vessels, they are intended for some service, that is, by the just ordering of their punishments they serve the use of the honorary vessels. He does not hate them, then, insofar as they are men or insofar as they are vessels, that is, he does not hate in them either their work of creation or their work of providential ordering, since he hates nothing of what he made. And in making them vessels of condemnation, he has his sights set on the service they provide for the correction of others. He hates in them the iniquity that he has not done; just as the judge hates theft in man, but not the condemnation of the thief to the work of the mines. The thief does the first thing; the second, the judge. Similarly, God, making the mass of the wicked vessels of condemnation, does not hate what he does, that is, the work of his penal ordination for the reprobate, with which he helps those he favors with his mercy to be saved. In this sense it was said to Pharaoh: For this reason I have exalted you, to show my power in you and to make my name known throughout the earth. This display of divine power and the proclamation of his name throughout the land instils holy fear and inspires a desire for correction in those who have been appropriately called. Accordingly, Saint Paul continues: If, in order to show his wrath and make his power known, he endured with much long-suffering the vessels of wrath, fit for perdition, who are you to ask God for an account? Relating these words to the previous ones, here is their meaning: If God, to manifest his justice, has endured the vessels of condemnation, who are you to ask him for a reason?

And he not only says that, wanting to manifest his wrath and make his power known, he endured with great patience the vessels of wrath, fit for perdition, but he adds that his purpose was to display the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy. What benefits the vessels that are to be condemned?

Others he cursed and humiliated and cast down from their place. As the clay in the hands of the potter, who determines its destiny according to his will, so are men in the hands of their Maker, who makes them according to his will. In front of evil is good, and in front of death, life; thus, in front of the just, the sinner. Consider in this way all the works of the Almighty, two by two, one facing the other. Prophecy of an intellectual nature is presented in a way when the meaning of the images and the purpose to which they are ordered are known by revelation. This is the surest kind of prophecy and to which the Apostle gives the name of such. Thus Joseph deserved to understand what was a dark vision for Pharaoh, and Daniel explained to the king what he had seen without understanding it. For God uses evil spirits as ministers to execute his wrath on the evil and test the good, although in different ways in both cases. For although an evil spirit is evil because of its evil will to harm, yet even this same faculty of harm is subordinate to Him under whose power all things are arranged according to certain and just degrees of merit. Because just as no evil will comes from God, so there is no power that does not come from Him. And although each person is free to will what he pleases, it is not, however, in the power of one person what he can do to anyone else or what he can suffer from him. For the only Son of God himself, being ready to suffer for a certain time, humbly responded to the proud words of a man who assumed the power to kill him or set him free: You would not have, he said, any power over me if it had not been given to you from above. The devil also, wanting to harm the holy man Job—and in truth he did not lack the will to do so—nevertheless asked permission of the sovereign God, saying: Stretch out your hand and touch him in his flesh, although, having obtained permission, he had to do this himself. It was a way of asking for permission, and after having obtained it, the hand of the Lord called upon his own hand, that is, the same power that he wanted to receive. This agrees with what is in the Gospel, where the Lord said to the disciples: Satan has sought you this night to destroy you like wheat. Thus, then, it was called the evil spirit of God, that is, God's instrument to execute on Saul the punishment that he should bear according to the judgment of the almighty Judge. Therefore, when we hear that God says: I am repentant, let us examine what man's repentance consists of. In him the will to change certainly dominates, but in man it is accompanied by pain, since he reproaches himself for having acted recklessly. Let us eliminate these imperfections, attached to human weakness and ignorance, and let us abandon the pure will to change a thing so that it is not as it has been until now; Thus we can somehow glimpse how divine repentance should be understood. For when it is said that God repents, he expresses his will that a thing should not continue to be what it was when he made it, and yet, when it was like that, it is because it should be; and when it is not allowed to be what it was, it is because it should no longer be, as God determines with an eternal, calm and just judgment, and by his immutable will he orders everything that is subject to change. 5. But since we usually speak with praise of the knowledge and prescience of man, and the human race usually fears rather than rebukes anger in the very powerful, we believe that such concepts suit God. But as for zeal and repentance, since the first is considered guilty and the second supposes a fault that must be corrected, and therefore both things involve a reproach for men, we are surprised to read that similar affections are attributed to God. But Holy Scripture, which looks after the good of all, still appropriates these things to God, so that we may also refine those more adequate concepts attributed to him and purify them from the imperfections with which they are enveloped in human language. For through these things that we dislike to put in God, just as they are found in men, we also learn to purify the concepts that we believed were most appropriate and convenient for the divine being. But in this fact an even easier solution and a simpler interpretation can be given, believing that it was not really the spirit of Samuel evoked from his rest, but some ghost or imaginary illusion formed by the devil, to which the Holy Scripture gives the name of Samuel, because the names of what they represent are ordinarily given to the images. In painted pictures, in statues made of metal, wood or any other material suitable for this type of work, and the same in the appearances of dreams, the names of the things of which they are images are used. Who doesn't call a portrait of a man a man? When we see some portraits of men, without hesitation we apply their proper names to them; Thus, in the presence of a painting or a gallery of pictures we say: that one is Cicero, that one Sallust, the other Aquiks and the other Hector; here is the river Simois, that is Rome; and they are nothing but painted images. Those statues of cherubs that God ordered to be placed on the ark with high symbolism, even though they are heavenly powers, are frequently called cherubs in the Holy Scriptures. In the imaginary visions of dreams, the person who has them does not say: I saw the image of Augustine or Simplician, but I saw Augustine or Simplician, although we were unaware of it at the time of having such representations: so evident is it that we do not see the people themselves, but their images. Pharaoh says that he saw ears of grain and cows in his dreams, not their images.

If, then, we certainly know that we give images the names of the things they represent, it is not surprising that the Holy Scripture speaks of Samuel's vision, although perhaps only his image appeared, by art.

In the question that you propose to me about that passage of Scripture: King David entered and sat before the Lord, what can be the meaning of these words except that he sat in the presence of the Lord, be it where the ark of the testameate was, by which a more sacred and reverential presence of the Lord can be taken; Whether he sat down to pray, which cannot be done well except in the presence of God, that is, in the depths of the heart? The aforementioned expression before the Lord could be interpreted for a place where there was no man to witness his prayer. Pray, then, for the sake of the ark of the testament, pray for having chosen a secret place far from any witness, pray for the retreat into the intimacy of his heart, where the fervor of the praying person was, it was well said: He sat before the Lord. Unless we find it strange that David prayed sitting down, something that Elijah also did when he obtained rain with his prayer. These examples teach us that there is no prescribed bodily posture for prayer, provided the spirit, placed in the divine presence, fulfills its intention. For we pray standing, as it is written: But the publican stood retired; We pray on our knees, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, and sitting, according to the examples of David and Elijah. And if we did not pray even while lying down, it would not be said in the Psalm: Every night I will wash my bed and water my footstool with tears. Indeed, when one wants to pray, he places his body and takes, according to the circumstances of the time, the most convenient position to awaken devotion. But when we do not go to prayer on purpose, but a lively desire to pray overtakes us, that is, when some pious effect suddenly comes to mind that moves us to supplicate with unspeakable groans, however we find it.

2. Prohibition, stimulant of desire (I, i, 5).—It is a vulgar observation of psychology how the prohibition of a thing quickens and ignites curiosity and desire for what is forbidden. The forbidden fruit has a bittersweet flavor that enchants and seduces. Saint Augustine points out this psychological fact in human falls. Already in the first temptation, to which Eve gave in, this factor intervenes: Suasio delectationis ad peccandum vehementior est, cuín adcst prohibitio (De div. quaest. 83, q. 66, 5: P L 40, 63). With the prohibition, desire increases, when liberating grace is lacking: Augetur enim prohibitione concupiscentia, quando deest gratia liberantis (Quarumd. Propos. ex Ep. ad Romanos, XXXVII: P L 35, 2070).

i. The law and grace (I, i, 2).—Julian reproached Saint Augustine for having used derogatory language with respect to the law in favor of grace: "I put aside the furious rage with which you attack the entire law, believing that it commanded mortals things beyond their reach and power": Taceo interim qua rabie in totam legem fremas, quam creáis ea imperasse mortalibus, quorum apud eos nullam facultatem videret (Opus imp., III, 116: P L 45, 1297). Such a reproach is unfounded, since the holy Doctor, when speaking about the law, does so in the same terms used by his teacher, Saint Paul. I have already indicated before that the Augustinian doctrine is equidistant from two extremes: Manichaeism and Pelagianism. For the Manichaeans, the law was perverse, the work of an evil spirit. Against them, Saint Augustine defends the essential goodness, the sanctity and usefulness of the law and the value of the Old Testament, as a guide and preparation for the New. Le3- does not cure the disease, but it diagnoses it; It does not heal the sore, but rather pokes it in a certain way, so that its sting forces us to seek medicine. The Pelagians used a contrary and hyperbolic language to defend the law, identifying it with grace. In this they showed their self-righteous mentality. The law is enough to do good without the need for any higher help. She is help and strength and the only safe bastion for man. Against this language, which rendered the New Covenant useless and annulled redemption and the mystery of the cross, Saint Augustine proclaims the distinction and supremacy of the grace of Jesus Christ. We must distinguish law and grace, says the Saint. The law knows how to command; grace, help. Neither the law would command if there were no will nor would grace help if the command were sufficient: Vis-, tinguenda es lex et gratia. Lex iubere novit, gratia iuvare. Nec lex iuberet, nisi esset voluntas, nec gratia iuvaret, si sat esset voluntas (Epist. 177, 5: P L 33, 766). Saint Augustine does not lower or belittle the law, but rather declares its impotence to sanctify man, the same as Saint Paul in the Epistle to the Romans, where he demonstrates two things: the law did not make the Jews better, because they were content with its crust and exteriority; Neither the perfection nor the benefit of faith and the Gospel is a salary due to legal practices and observances, but a pure gift from God, that is, grace.

In this sense it is said that the law was an encouragement to sin. 3. Carnal and spiritual (I, 1, 7).—Spiritualization is the work of a divine force that transforms the carnal man. As Saint Augustine indicates in this place, this renewal requires three things: the forgiveness of sins (gratia donor peccata), the progressive illumination of the spirit (luminc vegetátus) and the affective change that love brings about (infundente spiritum caritatis). No other spiritualism—Hinduism, Islam, Theosophism, etc.—can bear the authentic seal of truth. No matter how much we talk about the spirit, deep down the flesh rages, that is, the old man, powerless to renew himself and proud of his own strength, if he is not renewed in Christ. The ideal of the Catholic spiritual life reaches its apex in what Saint Augustine calls iucunda iustitia, the glad love of justice. The softer and more pleasant the law of justice is, the more spiritual man becomes. But note that he does not admit for the current existence of Christians a perfect spiritualism, which is reserved for the glory and joy of the resurrection. The flesh testifies its presence in this world even in the most perfect spirits, such as the saints. 4. It is like a loving conception, - in which the Mother of all believers introduces them into her womb, catechizing them, exorcising them and testing them: catechizantur, exorcizantitr, scrutantur (De fide et operibus, VI, 8: P L 40, 202). Above all, the solemn anointing of the cross on the forehead was the sign of belonging to a great family: Et quod signum crucis habímí in fronte catechumeni, iam de domo magna sunt (In loan., tr. 11, 4: P L 35, 1476). This was like entry into the womb of the Church: See signum crucis in utero matris concepti cstis, says the author of a sermon attributed to Saint Augustine (De symb. ad cai., I, 1: P L 40, 637). But the gratuitousness of the privilege granted to Jacob shines even with the modern lesson. 11. The example of Esau and Jacob (I, 2, 3).—According to modern commentators, the context of the passages analyzed by Saint Augustine considers Rebekah's twins as heads of two peoples and not as individuals. For the Doctor of Grace, however, they embody two types of humanity: the elect and the reprobate. But if we consider that the eldership transferred to Jacob is related to the messianic privileges of his descendants, denied to that of Esau, the accommodation of those two types to the two great groups into which the citizens of the future kingdom of the city of God will also be divided becomes very reasonable.

The hardness of Pharaoh (I, 2, 15).—The hardening on the part of God is reduced to a permission, to a not wanting to be pitied. It is not the sun that freezes the water with its action, but the removal of its heat. In itself, the human spirit, separated from the light and warmth of God, darkens and freezes. Hardening is called spiritual freezing, its type in Holy Scripture being Pharaoh, who resisted the divine call on behalf of the Israelites. The positive and true cause of hardening is in freedom, which distances itself from God. «The use of free will should not be annulled, because Scripture says in several places: I hardened Pharaoh, or I will harden Pharaoh's heart (Ex. 4, 21; 10, 1). For that did not mean that Pharaoh himself stopped hardening his heart: Non enim propterea ipse Pharao non induravit cor suum. Considering this fact, it is also read in Scripture, after the plague of mosquitoes was gone: Pharaoh hardened his heart and did not want to free the people. Thus, God hardened by righteous judgment, and Pharaoh himself hardened by his free will (De gratia et lib. arb., XXIII,. 45: P L 44, 911). Note the difference between this doctrine and that of the reformers, such as Calvin, who admitted a more positive action in the punishment of the Egyptian tyrant: An induravit non emolliendo 1 Id quidem verum est: sed plus aliquid fecit quod obstinatione pectus chis obfirmandum Satanae tradidit (Instit., I I, c. 4, § 4 ).

Ineffective Vocation (I, 2, 13).—Vocatio... qua moveri non possent. The Saint distinguishes two vocations: one secundum propositum, secundum consilium voluntatis divinae, and it is founded on the absolute and effective will to save those he calls. It is also called a suitable or congruent vocation, because those called correspond to it. But there is another vocation with which men cannot be moved; It is ineffective and detached from the consent of the creature to the will of the Creator. Just as the vocatio secundum propositum is ejectrix bonae voluntatis, it produces the desire to respond to the call, in the second such effect is not followed, undoubtedly due to the obstacles placed by human wills. The Saint seems to indicate this with the words: Non congruebant ñeque contemplabantur vocationi. Divine help is frequently contrasted by the stubbornness of the wicked. A force sufficient to move a man or a mass can be contrasted by a contrary action or a resistance that nullifies what is intended. For the divine vocation finds limits and resistance in free will, tyrannized by passions. Of many it can be said what the Gospel of the Jews affirms: that they could not believe.

Sin V. the penalty of sin (I, 2, 18).—This comparison of the judge who hates theft and punishes it has become classic, to explain the divine conduct in the condemnation of sinners, in which two things must be distinguished: guilt, that is, inordinatio et perversitas, the disorder and perversity, to which man has voluntarily adhered, and the opus ordinationis suae, or the penalty. due. God hates all sin, like the upright judge the murder or theft that he must investigate, and does not want the condemnation of the sinner; But, once the crime is committed, both human and divine judges determine and impose the just punishment. In this sense the words of Saint Augustine must be understood when he says that God tacit vasa in contumeliam. In every condemned person there are positive and good elements, annexed to his nature, which are the work of the Creator: there are also elements of p-ivation, that is, impiety and malice, for which he is subjected to a determined punishment and dear Lord El. The ears, both in the horn and in the spirit, are the work of the Creator; but the culpable deprivation of the sight of God or the culpable renunciation of his eternal vision, postponing it to the enjoyment of creatures (disorder, perversity, mortal sin), is the work of free will; and the eternal deprivation of the sight of God, deserved by voluntary turning away from Him, is a penalty determined by infinite justice. 22. Essence of sin (I, 2, 18).—The definition of sin given here by Saint Augustine has also become classic among theologians and spiritual writers: A praestantiore Condltore aversio et ad condita inferiora conversio. It is also usually repeated in this form: Aversio a Deo et conversio ad creaturas. It involves two constitutive elements: the formal and the material. The formal aspect of sin is the separation or abandonment of God, to enjoy, against his will, creatures. Conversion particularly addresses two terms: the enjoyment of one's own spirit and its independence and that of bodily goods. Thus, the two peculiar forms in which all sin is coded are pride and sensuality. That is why we understand how God cannot be the author of sin or positively influence it. Metaphysically, it is repugnant for God to encourage anyone to sin, that is, to separate and depart from Him, favoring creatures. A God who did this would be a contradictio in terminís.

As human eyes are not helped by light so as not to see, but for vision its help is absolutely necessary, so God, who is the light of the inner man, has a part and cooperates in acts done according to the norms of true justice. Certainly, answers the holy Doctor: with divine help and human cooperation, irreproachable justice can be achieved. But has anyone really achieved such perfection? The first is a question of possibility; the second, a question of fact, affirmed as real by the Pelagians.

Those who say that Adam was created in such a way that he would have died even without sinning, not as a punishment for his guilt, but because of the necessity of his nature, undoubtedly insist on applying, not to bodily death, but to that of the soul, which is contracted by sinning, what is written in the law: On the day you eat, you will surely die. With that kind of death the Lord indicated that the unbelievers were dead, of whom he says: Let the dead bury the dead. But what will they respond to the passage where we read what the Lord said to the first man after sin, rebuking and condemning him: You are earth and you will become earth? Well, evidently, not because of the soul, but because of the body, it was earth, and with bodily death it had to turn to dust. Notwithstanding that, even though he was bodily earth and preserved this animal body in which he was created, if he had not sinned, he would have been transformed into a spiritual body, to achieve without danger of death the state of incorruption promised to the figles and the saints. And not only do we feel in ourselves the desire for this incorruption, but the Apostle makes it known to us, when he warns us and says: Because, while we were here, we groaned, longing to put on our heavenly abode, so long as we were found clothed, not naked. Because those of us who are in this tent groan, overwhelmed, because we do not want to be stripped, but rather overdressed, so that this mortal thing may be absorbed by life. Therefore, if Adam had not sinned, he would not have been stripped of the body, but would have received a garment of immortality and incorruption, so that the mortal was absorbed by life, that is, passed from an animal condition to a spiritual one.

7. Although I fear that such an evident truth may be rather obscured by my explanations, nevertheless, notice the clarity of the Apostle's thought: If then Christ is in you, the body is certainly dead through sin, but the spirit possesses life because of righteousness. This was said so that men would not consider the benefit of Christ's grace to be illusory or of little value, since they necessarily had to undergo bodily death. But they must note that, although the body still carries the stigma of sin, which subjects it to death, nevertheless, the spirit, which had been extinguished in man with a kind of death, has already begun to live by the justice of faith, namely, infidelity. Do not believe, then, that the favor that has been given to you with the indwelling of Christ in you has been little, because in the body, dead through sin, the spirit now lives through justice; and so do not lose hope of bodily glorification either. For if no Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will likewise give life to your mortal bodies through the indwelling of the Spirit in you. Why do we want to obscure such copious light with the smoke of human disputes? The Apostle cries out: It is true that the body is dead in you because of sin; but the resurrection of your mortal bodies will come through the righteousness, by which the spirit now lives, and everything will be accomplished with the grace of Christ, that is, through the indwelling of the Spirit in you. And you still want to make complaints? He also adds how the spirit, mortifying the body, spiritualizes and vivifies it: Ea, pwss, brothers, he says, we are debtors, but not to the flesh, to live according to it; because if you live carnally, you will die; But if you mortify the actions of the flesh for the sake of the spirit, you will live. Which is like saying: If you live following the inclinations of the dead body, everything will die; but if you live according to the spirit, mortifying the flesh, everything will flourish with life.

What is this antithesis of a judgment that condemns us for a single sin and a grace that justifies us of many sins? On the hypothesis that there is no original sin, does it not follow that the same extends the object of * justification by grace, and that of the judgment of condemnation for many crimes? Because neither grace forgives nor justice condemns many crimes. And if, therefore, a single sin is a title of condemnation, since all the crimes on which the condemnation has fallen were committed in imitation of that one, for the same reason we should admit that justification falls only on one sin, since all those that are forgiven to those justified were also committed in imitation of that one. But this is not the feeling of Saint Paul, when he said: Through one man's sin came condemnation, but grace, after many transgressions, brought justification. Rather, let us penetrate the thought of the Apostle and convince ourselves that he understands the condemnatory judgment for a crime, because original sin alone would be enough for men to condemn themselves, even if they had no others. And although those who added their own sins to the original will be judged with greater severity, and each one will receive the punishment proportional to them, nevertheless, even the simple sin of origin not only separates from the kingdom of God—where, according to the confession of the Pelagians themselves, children who die without having received the grace of Christ cannot enter—but also separates them from health and eternal life, since the kingdom of God and eternal life are one and the same thing, and are achieved through union with Christ.

And no one is reborn into the body of Christ unless he is first born into this body of sin. ABOUT how, then, using evil from a good is a sinful action, using good from evil is a praiseworthy action. These two things, good and evil, and the other two, good and bad use, combining them with each other, give rise to four different actions. He who consecrates continence to God makes good use of a good; He who consecrates it to an idol misuses a good. He who seeks the satisfaction of his lust in adultery misuses an evil; He who restrains his concupiscence within the limits of marriage uses good for evil. For as the good use of a good is more praiseworthy than the good use of an evil, even though they are only good things, so he who gives his daughter for marriage does well, but he who does not give her does better. How can these things be verified? It must be answered how the spiritual regeneration can take place in men who come from the flesh by generation. After lightly pointing out the ignorance of the one who surpassed the others in the function of the teaching, and having rebuked the disbelief of those of his class, averse to the testimony of the truth, he added how He had spoken to them about things on earth, without giving them credit, asking and wondering how they would believe other, higher revelations. The spiritual generation, he says, will make men, from earthly, become heavenly; and they will not achieve this without becoming my members, so that the same one who came down ascends, because no one has ascended except the one who came down. For no one ascends into heaven except he who came down from it, the Son of man, who is in heaven; Therefore, to ascend it is absolutely essential that men, transformed and exalted, form unity with Christ, so that Christ himself, who descended, also ascends, identifying his Body or Church with himself, since the union of both is understood more truly than any other those words: They will be two in one flesh; and those that Jesus pronounced for the same purpose: Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. Despite this, he did not believe to lower his divinity—and to this end, without leaving heaven, he descended to earth—giving him the title of Son of Man, just as he deigned to grant his humanity the title of Son of God, provided that he avoids considering them as two Christs, one God and the other man, because one and the same Person is God and man: God, because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was in the bosom of God, and God was the Word; man, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Because of the distance between divinity and human weakness, the Son of God remained in heaven and the Son of man walked on the earth; but by virtue of the unity of person, by which the two natures form a single Christ, we can say that the Son of God also walked on the earth and even the Son of Man himself remained in heaven. Thus, the belief of the most incredible things guides us to the faith of those that are easiest to believe.

Great and wonderful dignity is this, which cannot be realized except by the forgiveness of sins, and for this reason it continues and says: Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so it is fitting that the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may not perish but may obtain eternal life. We know what happened in the desert: many died from snake bites; Then the people, confessing their sins, through the intercession of Moses, begged the Lord to deliver them from that plague; and Moses, at the command of God, lifted up the bronze serpent, and warned the people that all those infected with the poison should look up to it, and all who looked at it would be healed. What does this raised serpent mean if not the death of Christ, according to the figure in which the effect is represented by the cause? Because death comes from the serpent, because man has been persuaded of sin, for which he deserves to die. But the Lord did not transfer sin into his flesh, which is like the poison of a serpent; He did take death, so that the punishment without guilt would also reach his flesh, which had the likeness of sin, and in this way, through that apparently sinful flesh, sin and punishment would be abolished. Just as, then, he who contemplated the raised serpent was healed from poison and free from death.

68. Some will object: If the current state is not that of a pure nature, but the result of a lapsed nature, since Adam was not created in such conditions, why did Christ, much more excellent than him, born of a Virgin without the stain of any sin, manifest himself in the same conditions of weakness, procreation and development? We answer this difficulty: Adam was not created in the same conditions, because, not having a father who preceded him in sin, he was not begotten in the flesh of sin. Ours, however, is a different situation, because, because their sin has preceded us, we are children of sinful flesh. Christ also came in a state similar to ours, because he was born in the flesh with appearances of sin, in order to condemn sin as its victim. We are not dealing here with Adam in relation to his physical stature, because he was not created as a child, but with perfect bodily development. It can be said that animals also follow the same law of development, nor was it due to any sin of theirs that they came into this world lacking in robustness and corpulence. Now is not the time to explain that fact. It is about the vigor and discursive strength of Adam's soul, with which he could understand the imposition of a command and law from the Lord and easily comply with it if he wanted. But now he comes into this world with absolute impotence in this aspect, due to the frightful ignorance and weakness of the mind, not of the body, despite everyone recognizing that in infants lives a rational soul of the same nature as that of the first man. Furthermore: the same bodily weakness shows, in my opinion, the seal of a mysterious punishment. In adults who have reached the use of reason, the consent they give to sinfully give in to concupiscence is the work of their own will. And even when the total remission of sins has been achieved and the crime that had chained them from the beginning has been unleashed, concupiscence remains in them for the exercise of the struggle, without harming them at all—unless they consent to illicit things—until death is absorbed by victory and, with perfect pacification, there are no enemies left to defeat. Those who freely allow themselves to be dragged by it into illicit things are made guilty, and if they are not cured with the medicine of penance and works of mercy through the mediation of the divine Priest, who intercedes for us, it will lead them to the second death and damnation. Therefore the Lord, in teaching us to pray, commanded us to say: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors, and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For evil resides in our flesh, not by virtue of the nature it received from the hands of the Creator, but by the vice into which it voluntarily fell, losing its strength and wounding itself more easily than it can heal. The Apostle alludes to this evil with the words: I know that good does not dwell in my flesh. And he forbids us to consent to it: Let not sin reign* in your mortal body so that you follow its foolish desires. If, freely yielding to the perverse inclination, we have consented to the movements of carnal concupiscence, to cure ourselves of its effects, we say: Forgive us our debts; and we add the remedy of works of mercy by saying: As we forgive our debtors. To ward off consent, we ask for help saying: Do not lead us into temptation (or as some codices read: Do not lead us into temptation). Not that such temptations come to anyone from God: For God cannot be tempted to evil nor does He tempt anyone; but that, if perhaps our concupiscence begins to tempt us, we should not be deprived of the divine help with which we can overcome it, resisting its flattery.

5. God does not help us to sin, but without his help we cannot carry out righteous works or fully fulfill the precept of justice. Because just as the eyes of our body do not need the help of light in order not to see, closing and turning away from it, on the other hand, to see something its influence is required and without it vision is impossible, in the same way, God, who is the light of the inner man, acts in the gaze of our soul, so that we do good, according to the norms of his justice, not according to our own. It is our thing to turn away from Him, and then we act according to the wisdom of the flesh; then we consent to carnal lust in unlawful things. When we turn to God, He helps us; When we turn away from Him, He abandons us. He helps us in the work of our conversion, which the light in the bodily eyes certainly does not do. When, then, He commands us, saying: Turn to me and I will return to you, and we pray to Him: Turn us, O God of salvation!; and God of virtues convert us, we only ask this: Give us what you command us. When He imposes this precept on us: Understand, you foolish people, and we beg Him: Give me Understanding to know your commandments, we also tell Him the same thing: Give us what you command. When He commands us and says: Do not follow your evil desires, and we respond: We know that no one can be continent if God does not grant it to him, we make the same request: Give us what you command. •When he commands saying: Do justice, and we beg him: Teach me the precepts of your justice, we repeat the same prayer: Give us what you command. And when he tells us: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled, from whom should we ask for the food and drink of righteousness, but from him who promises his fill to the hungry and thirsty? Less thick were the darkness that blinded the Pharisee, who truly erred, believing that no more degree could be added to his justice and taking pleasure in having reached its fullness; But he even thanked God that he was not like other men, unjust, thieves, adulterers, nor like the publican, and that he fasted twice a week and gave tithes of everything he owned. He did not ask for any increase in justice for himself, but for the goods he had he was grateful to God and confessed to having received them all from Him; and, nevertheless, he was condemned, either because, as if he were fed up, he did not ask for other delicacies of justice for himself, or also because he gloried in insultingly putting himself before the publican, who hungered and thirsted for it. What will he do, then, with the men who, although they do not boast of possessing justice or at least its fullness, nevertheless harbor the presumption of believing that they must have it as their own harvest and not ask for it from their Creator, in whom is the granary and the source of it? Which does not mean that we must be content at this point with desires alone, but rather add the effective effort of our own will. In fact, God is called our helper, and no one can be helped without putting in some of their own effort. For God does not work salvation in us as if we were insensitive stones or beings in which nature has not placed its reason and will. But why does it help one and not another, why this one more and the other less, so-and-so in one way and so-and-so in another? In Him is the arcanum of such unfathomable justice and the sovereignty of infinite power.

After the prophet said: I said: I will confess my sin to God and you forgave my iniquity, he then added: Because of this need all the saints will call upon you at an opportune time. It does not say all sinners, but all saints, because this is the voice of the saints: If we say that we do not have sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. Also in the Apocalypse Saint John tells us about those one hundred and forty-four thousand saints who did not defile themselves with women, but remained virgins, in whose mouth no lie was found, because they are blameless; undoubtedly blameless because they sincerely rebuked themselves; and therefore no lie was found in their mouth, because, if they said that there was no sin in them, they would deceive themselves and the truth would not be on their side; and certainly lies would reign where there was no truth, because the righteous man, when he begins to speak and accuses himself, does not lie. 9. Taking into account the above, those who rely on this text or other similar ones err greatly in the interpretation of the Holy Scripture: He who is born of God does not sin, nor can he sin, because the seed of God is in Him. They do not realize that each one becomes a child of God as soon as he begins to clothe himself with a new spirit and to be renewed according to the inner man, created in the image of his Maker. But the old one does not disappear from the hour of baptism. weakness: Renewal begins by the forgiveness of sins and by the savoring of spiritual things in those who already have a taste for them. The other effects are carried out in hope, until reality comes, until the body itself achieves its transformation into a perfect state of immortality and incorruption, which it will clothe when the dead are resurrected. And what meaning does this rebuke have, which we understand comes from the person of the Lord, Jesus Christ? He enumerates to him the great wonders that he works with his power, and on this basis he bases his reproach, as if saying to him: Can you perhaps work the wonders that I work? What do these words mean if not to make the holy patriarch (who foresaw by divine revelation that Christ would come to suffer for men) understand with what resignation he must endure his labors, since Christ, having become man for us, contracted no stain of sin and, being endowed with divine power, did not refuse obedience to the torments of the passion? Job himself understood it this way with his uplifted and pure spirit, adding these words to his response: I only knew you by hearsay, but now my eyes have seen you. For everything I recant and do penance among the dust and ashes. Therefore I condemned myself, and humbled myself, and was more reputed to be dust and ashes. 26. Let us now come to the third question. If man can be found without sinning in this life, with the help of God's grace, lent to the human will, why does no one achieve it? This can be answered very easily and truthfully: Because men do not want to. If you ask me why they don't want to, the answer would take us far away. But even to this I will answer in a few words, without advancing a more diligent examination. Men do not want to do what is right, either because they do not know what it is or because they do not find pleasure in it. For the will moves towards an object with greater affection, the better it knows its goodness and the greater delight its possession gives us. Ignorance, then, and weakness are the vices that paralyze the will to do a good work or abstain from a bad one. But that what was hidden is made known to us and that we become fond of what did not attract us before, is the work of the grace of God, which helps the wills of men; and in these lies, and not in God, the cause of not receiving divine help, whether it be those who are destined for condemnation for their unjust pride, or those who, despite their pride, must be corrected and instructed, if they are children of mercy. Therefore, Jeremiah, after saying: Lord, I well know that it is not in the power of man to determine his way, nor can anyone determine his path through it with equity, adds immediately: But correct me, O Lord, gently,

28. But men insist on investigating in the sphere of our will the portion of good that corresponds to us, and that does not come from God; I do not know how it can be found. Let us ignore for now what the Apostle assures when speaking of human goods: What do you have that you have not received? And if you received it, why do you pomp yourself as if you had not received it? The same reason also, as it can be applied to these problems within the restricted limits of our possibility, in investigating this problem, strongly urges us to defend divine grace, without annulling free will on the one hand, and without exaggerating its value on the other, so that with impious pride we appear to be ungrateful to the grace of God. 29. Thus, some have wanted to save the meaning of the Pauline text cited above by saying: "Everything that man has of good will must be attributed to God, because this could not even exist without man himself. Now, since God is the author of both existence and human nature, why not also attribute to Him everything that is good will, since this would have no reason to exist if the subject in which it resides is lacking?" But proceeding in this way, the bad will could equally be attributed to God, since it could not even be found in man if he did not exist. Thus, being a man comes from God; then also the bad will, because if it did not have a man in whom it would be seat, nor could it exist. And to say this is impiety. 30 But it must be affirmed that it can only come to us from God, not only the will of the will, by which it is inclined to one side or another and is counted among the natural goods of which we can make good or bad use, but also the good will, which belongs to the category of goods whose use cannot be bad; otherwise I do not know how the truth of the apostolic saying can be saved: What do you have that you have not received? a certain free will, which comes from God and can be good or bad, but the good will comes from ourselves, what comes from us is worth more than what comes from God. But this being absurd, then they must confess that we also get the good will from God. A strange thing seems to put the will in a middle ground, from God.

Let us remain within the limits of our wisdom and understand, if possible, how the sovereign God sometimes does not grant even to his saints either certain knowledge or the victorious delight of some good work, so that they may know that it does not come from them, but from Him, the light that illuminates their darkness and the gentle rain with which the land of His spirit bears fruit [21]. 33.! For when we ask God for help to do good and achieve the perfection of justice, what is the object of our supplication but to make us know what we were ignorant of and soften the practice of virtue, which previously repelled us? And his grace is also knowing what to ask for, which we did not know before; By his grace we have loved what previously did not attract us; and so, he who glories should not glory in himself, but in him Lord. Because standing up with pride is the work of human will, not of the grace of God, who does not move or help to conceive such feelings. Therefore, a certain appetite for self-domination precedes in man's will, which drives him to disobedience through pride. Without this appetite, nothing would be costly and without difficulty he could not have then wanted what he wanted; This vice turned out to be a justly due punishment, making submission to justice painful. And if God does not help us with his grace to overcome it, no one converts to justice; and unless healed by the operation of grace, no one enjoys the peace of righteousness. But to whom does this grace belong, which gives us victory and heals us, but to him who says: Convert us, O God of our salvation, and turn away your wrath from us? When he does so, he acts out of mercy, and it is necessary to exclaim: He does not punish us according to our sins, he does not repay us according to our iniquities. And those who don't do it, don't do it out of justice. And even then, who will dare to say, "Why have you acted like this?" to him whose mercy and justice the saints celebrate with pious sentiments? And this also explains how even his just and faithful servants are slow to cure them of some weaknesses, denying them the taste of goodness, which is necessary to fully practice all the precepts of justice, sometimes because they do not know what they should do, sometimes even knowing it; from which it follows that, according to the sovereign rule of truth, no

43. If anyone is still curious about why those who are born to baptized people are baptized, here is my brief answer. As the generation of sinful flesh through one, Adam, leads to condemnation all men who are generated in the same way, so the generation in a spirit of grace through one Mediator, Jesus Christ, leads to the justification of eternal life to all those predestined for regeneration. Now, the sacrament of baptism is, without a doubt, the sacrament that regenerates. Therefore, just as he who has not lived cannot die, and he who has not died cannot be resurrected, similarly there is no rebirth without birth. From which it follows that no one has been able to be reborn in his father without having been born first. It is necessary that even the infant be purified with the sacrament of regeneration, so that without it he does not have a bad death. However, everything else that is said there, if studied and examined with diligence and attention, as I have endeavored to do in the first of those two books, although the very nature of the matter necessarily engenders some obscurity of expression, does not admit any other meaning than that retained by ecclesiastical antiquity, it is appropriate to know: that faithful infants have obtained forgiveness of the sin of origin by the baptism of Christ.

As regards, he says, the matter of children, whom you have said should not be baptized on the second or third day after birth, because the ancient law of circumcision must be followed, and, according to it, you believe that no newborn child, before the end of the eighth day, should be baptized and sanctified, know that our council is very far from thinking like that. And, despite this, if even the greatest sinners who previously offended God greatly, when they have embraced faith, have all their sins forgiven and no one departs from baptism and receiving grace, with how much more reason should the newborn child not be prevented from carrying any other sin but the contagion of ancient death, contracted from the first birth by virtue of its carnal origin from Adam? He has easier access to forgiveness, for the same reason that he is forgiven, not his own sins, but those of others.
