11. Do you see how firmly this eminent man speaks, basing himself on the ancient and indubitable rule of faith? He published this very firm document to clarify with sure evidence a doubtful point about which the correspondent who wrote this had been consulted—and he reminded him that a conciliar decree had issued—so that no one would hesitate to baptize the child who was presented for this purpose even before the eighth day of birth. Well then, the council did not determine or confirm that children are linked to the bond of original sin, as if it were a new doctrine or one combated by others. The object of the discussion was different, and it was disputed over whether, taking into account the law of carnal circumcision, it was advisable to baptize children before the eighth day of birth. They all gave an affirmative answer, because it was not a point of consultation or questionable, but the loss of eternal salvation for the soul was considered absolutely certain and certain if it were to leave this world without receiving the sacrament, even if newborn children were only subject to the risk of original sin; and although forgiveness was easier for them, because they were the sins of others, it was no less necessary for that reason. With these very certain truths, that uncertain dispute over baptism on the eighth day was settled, with the council ruling that from the first day the salvation of the newborn should be looked out for, so that it would not perish eternally; and although the example of carnal circumcision was alleged, which was a shadow of future baptism, nevertheless the need to administer the sacrament on the eighth day should not be deduced from it, but rather spiritual circumcision is wrought in us by virtue of the resurrection of Christ, who certainly rose again on the third day after his passion; But if you look at the cycle of the days of the week, in which times unfold, he rose from the dead on the eighth day, or the first day after the Sabbath.

Observe here, I beg you, how Pelagius, being a man of great caution (since the previous words are copied from his book), felt the difficulty of the question of the origin of the soul. For he does not say that the soul is not produced by transmission, but "if the soul is not produced by transmission"; he did very well in using a dubious and non-categorical expression, in the case of a problem obscure, or for which we do not find or can very hardly find certain and clear testimonies in the divine Scripture. For the same reason I do not want to make reckless statements on this matter, and I ask: if the soul does not come by transmission, what justice is there when, after creating it immune from all sin, absolutely free from all contagion of guilt, it is condemned in infants to the disturbances and the most diverse torments of the flesh and even the assaults of the devil? Where is your victory, death? Where is your sting, death? But the sting of death is sin, and the force of sin is the law. He spoke of the resurrection of the body, when death will be swallowed up in victory, as this mortal body is clothed with immortality. Then death will be mocked, because, with the bodily resurrection, it will be destroyed by victory. Then it will be said to him: Where is your victory, death? Where is your sting, death? These words will be addressed to the death of the body, because it will be invaded by a victorious immortality when this mortal element is clothed with immortality. To death, I repeat, it will be said: Where, death, is your victory, which you extended to everyone in such a way that even the Son of God fought with you, and defeated you, not by avoiding you, but by embracing you? You conquered those who succumb to death; You were defeated in those who triumph with the resurrection. Temporary was the victory with which you subjected the bodies of mortals to your dominion; eternal will be our victory, for which you were devoured in the bodies of the resurrected. Where, then, is your sting, that is, the sin, with which we were pricked and poisoned, to the point of sticking into them and subjecting them for a long time to your power? But the sting of evil is sin, and the power of sin is the law. We all sin in one, so that we may all die in him; and we received the law, not to put an end to sin by amendment, but to increase it by transgressions. For the law entered so that sin would abound, and the Scripture put everything under the rule of sin. But we give thanks to God, who has given us victory through our Lord Jesus Christ, so that where crime abounded, grace abounded all the more, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ, and thus we might overcome death by immortal resurrection, and the sting of sin by free justification.

This is precisely what we preach against you; This is the nerve of all our controversy; We say that Adam, had he not sinned, would have been immortal according to his body; and you maintain that, sinning or not sinning, he would have died (Opus. imperf. contra luí., I, 68: PL 44, 1089-90). According to the holy Doctor, Adam was corruptible due to his bodily condition, incorruptible or immortal due to the grace of the Creator: Mortalis erat eonditione corporls anlmalis, im.mortalis autem benefit Conditoris (De Gen. ad litt., VI, 25, 36: PJL 34, 354). And this doctrine is defended here by the Saint: natural mortality and immortality by the grace of the Creator, if he remained submissive to his orders. That is why he possessed summa in carne sanitas, in animo tota tranquillit-as (De civ. Dei, XIV, 26: PL 42, 434). Thus now death is at the same time a natural condition of our physical existence and a penalty for the loss of grace, which was to preserve it from death. (Gf. SANIO THOMAS., Sum-zoa Theologica, 2, q. 164, a. 1 ad 1.) 2. The effects of justification (I, 9, 10).—Note the words that the Saint uses here when speaking of the effects of grace:. Gratia eius illuminationem iusiificationemque nostram intrinsecus operaUír. Sanctifying grace acts in what is endearing in nature: intrinsicus. Without a doubt, Saint Augustine speaks here of the grace called by theologians habitual, different from the current one, which consists of aids of illumination and gentle motions in the will to incite it to act justly. It is given to infants, incapable of receiving actual graces or of imitating anyone, as the Saint says, and grafts them into the Body of Christ. It vivifies everyone, and it also secretly infuses itself into infants: latenter infundit el parvulis. 3. Usque ad legem (I, io, 12).—St. Augustine interprets the words usque ad legem as a term of the Mosaic law; that is, the time that passes from Adam to Christ. But other ancient interpreters, and almost all modern ones, limit its meaning to the period from Adam to Moses. According to some, the Apostle's mind is that, before the law of Moses, original sin was as good as dead, without that formal rebellion against God and against the spirit to which the divine precept gave rise: Non concupisces. With such a command he revived man's sensuality. The passage is dark. (Cf. CORNELY, Comment. in h. 1.; BERAZA, Cursus theologicus. De Deo creante et elevante, n. 626.) 4. The condemnation of infants (I, 16, 21).—Saint Augustine expresses his opinion about the condemnation of children who die without baptism. It is not easy to know what the Saint means by damnatio omnium mitissima (De pee. mer. et remis.), damnatio omnium. levissima (Against luí., V,.11, 44: PL 44, 809). There has been no shortage of benign interpreters of his thought, denying that he defended the pain of meaning and reducing what they suffer to a slight sadness for the lost good of the beatific vision. However, it seems most likely that he subjected them to a very mitigated penalty of sense. Modern theologians take a more benign view on this point. Opinions on this matter can be classified into three groups. That of the supporters of the punishment of sense, called tortores infantium, like the Augustinian Gregory of Rimini; that of those who subject children to a slight penalty of sadness for the good they have lost, and that of those who admit a certain natural blessedness for them, without making them sharers in the vision of God.

The latter seems to be the opinion of Saint Thomas: Et ideo nihíl omnino dolebunt de carentia •visionis divinae: imtno magis gaudebunt de hoc quod participabunt multum de divina bonitote et perfectionibus naturalibits (In II Sent., dist. 33, q. 2, a. 2). However, theirs will always be a state of condemnation, for being deprived of a good that they could have achieved in other circumstances. 5. The gift of integrity (I, 16, 21).—Tune Corpus eius perdida gratiam: then his body lost grace. These words are understood above all from the so-called gift of integrity, which made the innocent man immune from concupiscence. The total submission of the lower appetites to reason and of the body to the soul was a privilege granted to Adam and Eve. With the loss of this gift, the instincts, previously submissive to the sovereignty of the spirit, went out of control, and the man began to feel a change in his entire being, a state of weakness and low rebellion, which testified to the seriousness of the fault committed.

However, do not forget that the disorder of the lower powers is not a formal sin as long as the will does not consent to it. 6. Sin and the temporality of man (I, 16, 21).—St. Augustine here attributes to sin not only mortality, but also temporality itself in very fundamental aspects. Sin has deeply temporalized men. The stabilltas aetatis, in which he was created, was succeeded by the mutabilitas aetatum, the change of ages, and the hasty race towards death: per mutabúuaws aetatum irent ín mortem. The ages are main milestones for the calculation of time in the current state of man, who became much more outdated and temporary in himself by losing the perpetual youth of grace, to which he was called, and by adhering to fleeting things, which with their comings and goings torment the spirit and wear out the best steel of the human heart. Non stat ergo aetas nostra: ubique fatiguetio est, ubique lassitudo, ubique corruptio (En. in ps. 62, 6: P L 36, 752). The time in which we now live is a process of degradation and destruction. Restlessness, opposed to the rest of eternity, and emotional mobility define the current situation of the human race. That is why sin, according to the mind of Saint Augustine, has a transcendental significance in the current course of history, because by it man was left abandoned to himself, at the mercy of the selfish and dispersive forces in which all guilty desertion of the Creator is ultimately resolved. 7. The Epistle to the Hebrews (I, 17, 50).—The Saint here considers the Epistle to the Hebrews as having an uncertain author, because, while in the Eastern Church they had it as canonical Scripture, due to the pen of Saint Paul, in the Latin Church its authenticity was discussed. Many did not accept it as a revealed book, according to Saint Jerome. (Cf. Catalogus Scriptorum ecclesiasticorum, c. 16.) In The City of God he is still perplexed about the true author: De quo (Melchisedech) in Epístola quae nunc inscribitur ad Hebraeos, qitam plures Apostoli Pauli esse dicunt, et magna conscripta sunt (De civ. Del, X V I, 22: P L 42, 500). But in the catalog of canonical books that he inserts in De doctrina christiana he attributes it to the Apostle, counting it among his 14 letters (De doct. christ., II, 8, 13: P L 34, 41). 8.

Eve and the serpent (I, 27, 55).—The words that Saint Augustine uses here: Serpenti credidit (Eve) ut libidine corrumperetur, were interpreted by Julian as if the Saint attributed the first carnal intercourse with the serpent to the woman. The words of Jesus, especially those he spoke at the Supper; The Gospels, the Epistles, the Acts of the Apostles, the Apocalypse, the Psalms and the prophetic books certify us of the necessity and fact of human salvation, operated by the Lamb of God, who erases the sins of the world. At the center of this divine process, whose effects the Saint expresses with the words: reconcile, incorporate Christi Corpori, vivificare, sals faceré, liberare, redimere, delere peccata, aluminare, is the sacrifice of the most merciful Redeemer: Non ergo reconcilian nisi peccatorum remissíone per unam gratiam misericordiosissimi Salvatoris, per unam victimam verissimi sacerdolis. Obedientia mentis (I, 29, 57).—Here Saint Augustine contrasts the primitive fall and redemption with the confrontation of Adam and Eve, of Jesus and Mary. The Mother of Jesus actively collaborated in the mystery of human salvation, not only in a physical sense, but also in a moral and spiritual sense. The obedient lie indicates Mary's perfect submission to the divine plan after the way in which the incarnation was to take place was revealed to her. There is like a double uterus and generation in the Virgin: the heart and the most pure entrails: FU prius adventus fidei in cor Virginis, et sequitnr fecundltas in uterus matris (Serin. 193, 1: P L 38, 1327). The Word of God is welcomed first in the heart and then in the bowels. Physical fertility follows the obedience and living faith of the Maiden of Nazareth.

In this spiritual principle, which so actively influences the generation of the Word, Saint Augustine usually mentions three virtues that have collaborated in the advent of the Son of God: faith, obedience, virginal purity, opposed to disbelief, disobedience and concupiscence, which caused the fall of the first parents. Therefore, as the Saint says, per mulierem- in interitum missi eramus, per mulierem nobis reedita est salus (Serm. 289, 2: P L 38, 1308). 11. The need for baptism for the remission of sins, the effects it produces, the rite of ablution and exsufflation, the exorbitations

The reception of the Eucharist is not necessary with a need for a means, but rather a divine and ecclesiastical precept for adults. Free will and mortal sin (II, 5, 5).—Against the Pelagians, according to whom free will is sufficient to fulfill the precepts of the law: Dicunt sufficere homini arbitrium ad dominica implenda mandata (Epist. 157: P L 33, 75), Saint Augustine always maintained the insufficiency of fallen man not to sin. «Sin is not a natural thing; But for the vitiated nature, which has made us children of wrath, the agency of the will is not enough to avoid it, unless it is healed with the help of grace through the work of our Lord Jesus Christ: Respondetur naturale non esse peccatum: sed naturae

praesertim vitiatae, measurement sumus facti My irae, parum esse ad non peccandum voluntatis arbitrium, nisi adiuta sanetur gratia Del per lesum Christum dominum nostrum {De periect. iustitiae, I I: P L 44. 293-4). Catholic theology has clarified the meaning of these assertions, distinguishing between the physical and moral power of human free will, which has the physical power to fulfill the commandments of the natural law, but is morally powerless to fulfill it all. The law of continence exceeds the forces of free will and to fulfill it requires supernatural help. The fallen hunger cannot morally, without divine help, long keep all the natural law or overcome serious temptations. The root of this weakness and impotence must be sought in the dispossession of divine help and the strength of sinful habits, which become bossy in man. That is why a great disciple of Saint Augustine, Saint Prospero, says that our will is vague, uncertain, instabais, imperita, injirma ad efficiendum, jacilis ad audendum, in cupiditatibus caeca, in omnious túmida, curis anxia, suspicionibus inquieta, gloriae quam virtuhnm avklior, famee quam conscientiae diligentior, et per omnem sui experientiam miserior fruendo his, quae concupierit, quam carendo: nihil in suis habet viribus nisi periciUi facilitate-m, quoniam voluntas mutabilis, quae non ab incommutabili volúntate regitur, tanta citius propinquat iniquitati, quanto,' verius intenditur actioni (De vocationc gcntium. I, 6: PL 5L 652). Our will is wandering, vacillating, fickle, inexperienced, weak in acting, bold in undertaking, blind in its desires, swollen in everything: it walks in thorns of care, restless in suspicions, more eager for glory than for virtue, more attentive to fame than to conscience, and, as it has proven, it hungers more by enjoying the things it desires than by lacking them. From its harvest only danger is easy, because the capricious will that is not governed by the rule of the sovereign will, the more it applies itself to active life, the more risk it runs of losing itself in sin. 15.- The principle of human cooperation (II, 5, 6).—St. Augustine frequently emphasizes the fact of the collaboration of free will with grace.

Two forces, intimately mixed, complete the work of man's sanctification: one divine and the other human. Here he clearly states this truth again: God does not move men like stones or insensible things, but rather like being free, placing his very gentle hands on the springs of free will; that is, through illustrations of understanding and movement, with which he invites you to voluntarily do what He wants. «With grace God inspires the desire for good, so that he does not do it unwillingly, but with pleasure (Contra duas Epist. Pelag., II, 8: P L 44, 583). • The Creator and the creature act with twinned actions, like the one who, giving his hand to the fallen, helps him get up. This does not eliminate one's own effort, but rather strengthens it: Nec adiuvari

Human life is full of dangers and temptations, even for those who serve God: Etiam Deo servientes tentat error ut decipiat: tentat labor aut dolor ut frangat: tentat libido, ut accendal; tentat moeror ut stern-at: tentat typhus ut extollal. Et quis explicat omnia feslinanter quibusgravatur iugum super filios Adamt (Contra hü., IV, 16, 83: P L 44, 782). 17. The causes of sin (II, 17, 26).—The Saint speaks here of the formal, non-encent causes of sin, to speak in scholastic terms, and he reduces them to two: ignorance and weakness. There is blameless ignorance, which is also called invincible: Non tibi depulatur ad culpam quod invitus. you ignore sed quod negligis quaerere quod ignores (De lib. arb., I I I, 19: P L 32, 1297). Ignorance of what should be known, in those who can overcome it and do not do so, is a sin; and in those who cannot overcome it, the penalty of sin (Epist. ad Sixtum, 194, 27: P L 33, 883).

But to remedy both things—ignorance and weakness—adjuvant grace is given, either in the form of illumination of the understanding, or as a motion impressed on the will, so that it overcomes all the attractions of sin: Delectat enim peccare: nam si non delectaret, non ieront (Serm. 190, 7: 38, 877). The reluctance of justice that man feels comes from illnesses of the spirit: from languoribus animae. Pañis in fastidio est, et delectat venenum (ib.). The bread gives us nausea, and we perish from the poison. Grace reforms the inner palate and savors it with the taste of higher things. 18. The predestination of the damned (II, 17, 26).—Sive damnandi praedestinati sint propter iniquitatetn superbiae. Saint Augustine sometimes speaks of the predestination of the damned, and his thoughts must be clarified by the doctrine he teaches elsewhere. From very early on, certain passages in his books were interpreted by some as if they taught the positive and absolute predestination of the damned. Saint Fulgentius, a great disciple and defender of the doctrines of our Doctor, was forced to combat some errors of his contemporaries, such as Monimo. Saint Augustine does not defend a destiny and predestination to sin, as if he positively wanted someone's condemnation, but rather the foresight and determination of the penalty with which he must punish transgressors of his commands. As in a penal code the sanctions that must be imposed for certain crimes are foreseen and determined for the future (which does not mean that the legislator wants the transgression of the laws and the penalties attached to them), so in the mind of God the crimes that many of his creatures will commit are foreseen from all eternity and the penalties that they must suffer for them are determined. In this sense we can speak of predestination to condemnation: damnandi praedestinati. Thus Saint Fulgentius clarifies to Mononym the passage referred to here: Propter iniquitatem superbiae praedestinati dicuntur damnandi, quod pertinet ad iudicium, non depravandi, quod pertinet ad pgccatum (Ad Monimum, Ubri tres, I, 28: P L 65, 177).

The same should be interpreted in other passages that speak, for example, of some ad interitum praedestinatos: Nihil aliud accipiendum existimo de illo Sancti Augustini sermone quo <¡ad interitum quosdam praedestinatos» firmat, nisi ad interitum supplicii, non delicti; ñeque ad malum quod iniuste admittunt, sed ad cruciatum, quem iustissime patientur (ib., I, 5: P L 65, 156). Such passages must be understood as referring to the prediction and determination of the penalty, not the crime; God does not predestine anyone to commit sins, but he does order the torment that they will justly suffer for them. 19. Exciting and adjuvant grace (II, 18, 31).—Divine grace is required for conversion; Quod ad Deum nos convertimus, nisi Ipso excitante alque adiuvante non possumus. When the creature responds to the call and breaks the dream and wants to do what is ordered, it also needs the help and strength of God; and such is the adjuvant grace. Delectatio victrix (II, ig, 32).—Jansenius forged the system of grace and its relations to free will with the theory of delectatio victrix, victorious delight, mentioned by Saint Augustine in this place. There are two delights: one earthly and the other heavenly; The first leads to sensual pleasures; the second, to the good. between the two

The elder, or superior in strength, wins, because the fallen man always acts moved by the spring of delight. The weight of delight determines all the decisions of free will, the same as on the scales, it leans towards where there is more weight. And this heavenly delight, as the determining cause of the movements of free will, is actus quidam indeliberatiis caelitus inmzissus in voluntatem, per quem ci bonum propositmn suaviter placel (De gratia Christi, IV, 11). Serious errors cloud this interpretation of the system of grace: first of all, the detertnism with which the two delights operate, with a decrease in freedom. human. Hence the condemned proposition: Interiori gratiae in statu naturae lapsae nunquam resistitur. Saint Augustine does not conceive the action of grace in this way: man sets many limits and in reality many times resists grace. Also with the doctrine of indeliberate movements it restricts and mutilates the action of God in the divine government of souls. That indeliberate movements appear in many of his interventions is beyond doubt for the holy Doctor. Particularly they take place in the awakening of the flavors or in the exciting grace, which can present attractions or incentives that gently move the will to want a thing, or also move man with fears and terrors. Both in the initial moments of conversion and in the process of sanctification, God now uses the attractions and delicacies of delight; now of the healthy fear it inspires, the saluberrimus terror of which it speaks. Severilate Dei corda mortalimn salubérrimo terrore quatiuntur (De cat. rud., V, 9: P L 40, 316). In the initium-fidei this healthy fear frequently intervenes: "For it rarely happens, or rather never, that he who comes with the desire to become a Christian does not come wounded by some fear": Rarissime quippe accidit mine vero nunquam, ut quisquam venial v.olens fieri christianus, qui non sit aliquo timore perculsus (De cat. rud., V, 9: P L 40, 316). And in another famous passage, to quell every movement of presumption in those who observe better behavior than others, he puts these words in the mouth of God: «You were not an adulterer; It's that I ruled you for me, I kept you for me. To commit adultery, you lacked a bad counselor. I made sure you didn't have it. (You did not find time or place. I made you have them. You had a bad advisor, you did not lack place or time.

Ut consentires ego terrui; So that you would not consent, I restrained you with my terror. Recognize, therefore, the grace of God, to whom you still owe not having committed certain sins” (Serm, 99, 6: P L 38, 598). To explain the transmission of original sin, Saint Augustine appeals to the mysterious solidarity of all men with the common father. It does not resort to the inclusion of all wills in Adam's will, but to the unity of nature, to seminal reason, to the condition of Adam, as head of the human race, who received and lost for all the privileges of his innocent state. The link that Saint Augustine establishes between Adam and his descendants is both biological and moral. In the year 418, Pope Saint Zosimus directed the bishops of the Catholic world to subscribe an epistle known as Ttfuctoria, in which he condemned Ceiestius and Pelagius and the Pelagian errors. The bishops also subscribed to it, except Julian of Eclana and seventeen other bishops of Italy, who refused to sign under the false pretext that Ceiestius and Pelagius, in addition to having rejected in their books the errors imputed to them, had been condemned without having been heard. Julian and his henchmen were, therefore, deposed and banished, and, although they wanted to assert civil authority in their favor, they followed nothing and persisted in their rebellion and in the propaganda of their heretical doctrines. To this time belong the two epistles of the Pelagians that Saint Augustine refuted in the year 42d •em the work, divided into four books, Contra duas chistóla? pelagianorum, dedicated to the successor of Zosimus, Saint Boniface, who had sent a copy of these epistles to the Bishop of Hippo. The first of these epistles was said to have been written by Julian of Eclana to confirm his supporters in Rome in the Pelagian doctrines and to attract new adhesions; The second, signed by eighteen Pelagian bishops, was addressed to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, with the aim of attracting him to his party. In the first book of his work Contra duas epistolas pelagianorwm, Saint Augustine responds with a copy of doctrine and great dialectical vigor to the slanderous statements that Julian attributes to Catholics, namely: that through the sin of Adam E, he lost his free will; that marriage is the work of the devil, and how many men are born are also the work of the devil; that all the apostles were always dominated by disordered concupiscence; that Little Bear was not immune from sin; that baptism does not forgive all sins nor erase guilt, but rather removes them, the root of all sins remaining in the flesh. In the second book, the Doctor of Grace begins the reply to the "pistol sent by the Pelagians to the bishop of Thessaloniki. MODESTY AFTER SIN

32. Well, tunics were not made to cover the entire body after sin, but rather sashes, which some of our translators have poorly interpreted as a covering. Which, without a doubt, is true; but cover is a generic name that can mean all types of clothing and cover. And for this reason this ambiguity had to be avoided, so that, just as the Greek text put perizomata, with which only the private parts are covered, so the Latin text had to put, either the same Greek word that is ordinarily used instead of the Latin one, or, as some have said, girdles, or better, according to others, campestria. Because this name has its origin in the fact that young people covered their private parts, according to the ancient Roman custom, when they trained naked in the field; which is why even today the name campestrati is given to those who cover that part of the body with a girdle. Furthermore, if after the sin they had to cover those parts with which they sinned, they should not have worn tunics, but rather covered their hand and mouth, because they sinned by stretching out their hand and eating. How is it, then, that, having taken the forbidden food and already committed the sin, one's gaze is fixed on those parts? What ignored novelty can be seen there that forces us to pay attention to it? 2. The Manichaeans say that the good God is not the creator of all natures; The Pelagians teach that it is not God who is the purifier, savior and liberator in all ages of men. The Catholic faith contradicts both, defending, on the one hand, the creature of God against: the Manichaeans, so that it is not denied that any creature was created by God, and on the other hand, against the Pelagians, so that in all ages the lost human nature may be repaired. The Manichaeans condemn the lust of the flesh not as an accidental vice, but as if it were from eternity an evil nature; The Pelagians praise it as if it were no evil, but rather a natural good. The Catholic faith contradicts both, saying to the Manichaeans: "It is not nature, but sin"; and to the Pelagians: "It does not come from the Father, but from the world," so that the one and the other do not hinder it from being cured, as weak health is cured, the former ceasing to believe it incurable and the latter ceasing to praise it. The Manichaeans deny that the evil principle of free will came upon the good man; The Pelagians teach that even a bad man has free will enough to fulfill the holy commandments. The Catholic faith refutes some and others, saying to the former: God made man upright; and to these: If the Son gives you freedom, you will be truly free. The Manichaeans say that the soul is a particle of God and that it is subject to sin because of being mixed with an evil nature; The Pelagians affirm that the just soul is not a particle, but a creature of God, and that it has no sin even in this corruptible life. The Catholic faith refutes both, saying to the Manichaeans: One of two:

9. It now remains for us to examine what, summarized in a few words, they attribute to us in their letter; to which we give the following answer. We do not say that free will has perished in human nature due to the sin of Adam, but that it has power in men subject to the devil to sin; But it has no power to live well and piously if the same will is not freed by the grace of God and assisted in every good work of action, word and thought. We say that no one but God is the creator of those who are born, and that marriage has not been instituted by the devil, but by God; that all, however, are born in sin because of inherited sin, and are therefore subject to the devil until they are reborn in Christ. Nor do we admit fate under the name of grace when teaching that the grace of God is not preceded by any kind of merits of men. If some like to designate the will of omnipotent God with the name of fate, for our part we give in to profane verbiage, but we do not like to dispute over words. 10. Thinking more carefully about how it occurred to them to object to us admitting fate under the name of grace, I began to examine the words that follow. He, abhorring or pretending to abhor this doctrine, hastened to anathematize this doctrine with only his lips; but, as can be seen from the books that he later wrote and is evidenced by the affirmation of his followers, he kept it fallaciously in his heart until later what cunning had hidden through fear, audacity proclaimed in writing. And after this the Pelagian bishops are not afraid, or at least not ashamed, to send their letters to the Eastern bishops, reproaching us for being defenders of fate because we do not say that the grace of God is given according to our merits, which is what Pelagius, for fear of the Eastern bishops, did not dare to affirm and was forced to condemn.

Have you declared in this same epistle your opinion both regarding baptism and grace? For how come what you say about the baptism that is conferred on infants, not teaching you, being immediately before what you say about grace, what you should feel about grace? For these are your words: We confess that baptism is necessary in all ages, and that grace helps the good purpose of all men, but that to the man who resists it does not give the desire for virtue, because in God there is no acceptance of persons. I now pass over what you have said about grace in these words; Answer me why you say that baptism is necessary in all ages; decide why it is necessary for the little ones; undoubtedly because it confers some good on them, and this is not small or mediocre, but great. For, although you deny that they inherit original sin, which must be forgiven in baptism, you do not deny, but rather you teach, that with that bath of regeneration the children of men are adopted as children of God. Tell us, then: how many children died after being baptized into Christ, by virtue of what previous merits did they receive it? If you answer that they deserved it because of the piety of their parents, you will be answered: How is this good sometimes denied to the children of pious parents and granted to the children of the wicked? For it sometimes happens that the child born of religious parents is taken away at a tender age, and even barely born, by death, while the child born of enemies of Christ receives the baptism of Christ through the compassion of Christians; the baptized mother cries for the unbaptized child, while a chaste woman picks up to baptize the strange child abandoned by an immodest mother. Here there are surely no merits of the parents; There are none, as you confess, of the same children. Because we know that you do not have this belief about the human soul, that is, that it has lived somewhere before having this earthly body and has practiced some good or bad action by which it has earned this different treatment in the flesh. What, then, was it that achieved baptism for this child and denied it to that other? Are they subject to fate, since they have no merit? Or is there acceptance of people here in the Lord?

Because you have put both things: first fate, then the acceptance of people; so, since both things must be rejected, it follows that you admit merit against grace. Answer, then, regarding the merit of children, why some die with baptism, others without baptism, and how without parental merit they enjoy or lack such an excellent gift, that from children of men they are made children of God without any merit from their parents, without any merit.

We are dealing with the desire for good: if they claim that this has its beginning in us and that it is carried out by God, they will see what they respond to Saint Paul when he says: Not that by ourselves we are capable of thinking something as of ourselves, but that our capacity comes to us from God. 21. So God works in man many works that man does not do; But man does no work that God does not cause man to do. Therefore, the desire for good would not proceed in the man of God if it were not good; Well, if it is good, it cannot come in man except from God, the supreme and immutable good. For what is the desire for good but charity, of which the apostle Saint John speaks bluntly, saying: Love comes from God? Nor does its beginning come from us and its perfection from God, but, if it is charity, it proceeds entirely in us from God. May God free us from the folly of putting ourselves first in God's gifts and God second; because His mercy will prevent me, and He is the one of whom it is faithfully and truly sung: You preceded Him with blessings of sweetness. And what else can be better understood here than the desire for good that we have been talking about? Because you begin to wish yourself well when it begins to turn sweet. When good is practiced out of fear of punishment, not out of love for justice, then good is not practiced rightly; nor is what appearances show to be executed externally carried out in the heart when a man would want to execute it if he could do it with impunity. Therefore the blessing of sweetness is the grace of God, by which he works in us to delight us and to desire, that is, to love, what he commands us: if the Lord does not warn us with it, not only does it not take place, but it does not even begin with us. For if we cannot do anything without Him, we can neither begin nor carry out anything; because, if it is to begin, it has been said: His mercy will prevent me; and if it is carried out, it has been said: His mercy will follow me.

Wonderful, but true, the justice of the law does not fulfill the justice that is given in the law or proceeds from the law, but that which is in the spirit of grace. For the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in those who, as it is written, walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. The Apostle says that he was a man without blemish in the flesh, not in the spirit, regarding the justice that can be given in the law; and he says that the righteousness that comes from the law was his righteousness, not God's. We must understand, therefore, that the justice of the law is not fulfilled according to the justice that can be given in the law or that proceeds from the law, that is, according to the justice of man, but according to the justice that is given in the spirit of grace; therefore, according to the justice of God, that is, that which comes to the man of God. Which can be expressed more clearly and concisely by saying that the justice of the law is not fulfilled when the law commands and man obeys, as it were, with his own strength, but when the spirit helps, and the free will, but liberated by grace, obeys. Thus, the justice of the law consists in commanding what pleases God, prohibiting what displeases Him; Giving yourself justice in the law is serving the letter and not asking outside the letter for help to live well. 12. Let's continue. What good is it for them to praise free will, against the Manichaeans, quoting for this purpose the testimony of the prophet: If you agree and listen, you will eat the best of the country; But if you refuse and rebel, you will be devoured by the sword. Yes, rather than defending free will against the Manichaeans, what they do is exalt it against the Catholics? Because they interpret the words If you will and more you will hear as if the merit of subsequent grace were included in the same preceding will, and thus grace is no longer grace, since it is given as payment. If they understood the passage in question: If you will and will hear me, confessing that he prepares even the same good will of whom it is written: God disposes the will, they would cite this testimony as Catholics and not only would they victoriously refute the Manichean heresy, but, furthermore, they would not invent this new Pelagian heresy. 13. What good does it do you to praise free will by saying that grace helps the good purpose of every man? This could be given a Catholic meaning, if good purpose did not suppose merit to which the reward should be granted as a debt, not as a grace; but that they should understand and confess that the same good purpose, which grace later helps, could not exist in man if grace had not preceded. Because how can the good purpose be in the hands of man, if the mercy of the Lord is dispensed with, when the good will is precisely what God prepares? What after the words: That grace helps the good purpose of everything, they added: but without giving the desire for virtue to those who resist, could have an orthodox meaning if it were not said by those whose thoughts are well known. Because in favor of those who resist, the very grace of God ensures that they first hear the divine call, and then, when the resistance ceases, it kindles in them the desire for virtue. But always, for everything one does to please God, his mercy prevents him, which is what these do not admit, because they do not want to be Catholics, but Pelagians. Because proud impiety takes great pleasure in the fact that the very thing that it is forced to confess as a gift from God does not seem like a gift it receives, but rather payment, that is, it seems that they, the children of perdition and not of promise, have made themselves good and that God, after they have become good, has repaid them for this work with the due reward.

Finally, he judges that they must be baptized even before they are eight days old so that the souls of the children do not perish due to the contagion of the old death, contracted at the first birth. How do they perish, if those who are born even of faithful parents are not subject to the devil until they are reborn in Christ and, freed from the power of darkness, are translated into his kingdom? And who is it that says that the souls of those who are born must perish if they are not reborn? Well, none other than the one who so praises the Creator and the creature, the craftsman and the work, that, invoking the veneration due to the Creator himself, he rebukes and corrects the natural repugnance that keeps men from kissing newborn children, saying that, when kissing such tender children, one must think of the hands of God, which have just finished their work. Did he condemn nature or marriage by confessing original sin? By applying the bath of regeneration to the prisoner who is born from Adam, did he deny the God who created those who are born? Perhaps because, fearing that souls would perish at any age, he judged with the council of his colleagues that they should be released even before eight days after birth, did he condemn marriage, since it shows in the child born of marriage or adultery, but because he is a man, the hands still moist of God, worthy even of the kiss of peace?

If, then, the holy bishop and most glorious martyr Cyprian judged that the original sin of children should be healed with the medicine of Christ, leaving safe the praise of the creature, leaving safe the praise of marriage, why does the new plague, not daring to call this doctrine Manichean, dare to attribute to the Catholics, who defend this, a foreign crime in order to cover up its own crime? 26. Does this Saint, such a celebrated teacher of truth, deny the free will of men by making God the total cause of our virtuous life? Does it perhaps revile the law of God when it implies that man is not justified by virtue of it, since it declares that what it commands must be obtained from God with prayers? Does the name of grace mean fate, even though it says that we should boast of nothing, since nothing is ours? Does he perhaps believe, like these, that the Holy Spirit is the help of virtue in the sense that this virtue, which receives help from Him, comes from us, when, saying that nothing is ours, he brings to this purpose what the Apostle said: Well, what do you have that you have not received? Or does it say that a most excellent virtue, patience, has its beginning in us and is then helped by the Spirit of God, but rather does it say that it has its beginning and its origin in Him? Finally, he confesses that neither good purpose, nor the desire for virtue, nor good thoughts begin to exist in man without the grace of God, when he says that we should not boast of anything, since nothing is ours. What thing is so subject to free will as what the law says: that you should not worship idols or commit adultery or murder? These crimes and others like them are those that, if someone commits them, separate him from the communion of the body of Christ. And yet, if the blessed Cyprian thought that our will was enough not to commit them, he would not understand that we said in the prayer give us this day our daily bread in the sense that we ask that we not be separated from heavenly bread and communion because of a serious crime, separated from the body of Christ. Let these newly minted heretics answer what good precedent merits there are in the enemies of the Christian name. Because not only do they not have new merits, but they have terrible ones. And, despite this, Saint Cyprian understands that we say in prayer: Your will be done in heaven and on earth so that we may pray for them, which for that reason are designated with the name "earth." We pray, therefore, not only for those who do not want to, but also for those who resist and fight. What, then, is what we ask but that they go from not wanting to wanting, from resisting to consenting, from fighting to loving? And who is to do this except he of whom it is written: God disposes the will?
Let those, then, learn to be Catholics who, if they do not commit some sin or practice some good work, do not want to glory in the Lord, but in themselves.

INTRODUCTION

Saint Augustine has been called the hammer of heresy, a name that fits well with the Doctor of Grace because of the vigorous blows unleashed on heresy and the constant persistence with which he has crushed error until it is reduced to dust. Saint Augustine has been, among all the fighters that Christianity has had, the wisest and the most combative. As soon as he has known the adversary of the doctrine of the Church, he presents battle to him on all grounds and fights relentlessly against him with all weapons. Such was his style of combat against the Manichaean and Donatist heresies; such was the sustained struggle against the Pelagian heresy. The phiriform polemical activity of Saint Augustine against Pelagianism covers all the areas and strongholds in which heresy can be combated. It is the private conversation, the sermon preached to the faithful, the withering commentary, the letters addressed to people from the most diverse social position, without excluding heretics themselves, whose correction is sought with exquisite prudence. It is the uninterrupted series of books of profound theological speculation or refutation of heretical writings. It is participation in the African councils, assemblies as well as decisive battles in the fight against heresy, and which reflect the heart and intelligence of Saint Augustine. These are the trips undertaken, despite his precarious health, when the good of the Church requires it, committed to the fight against its enemies. It is even the disclosure and commentary of public documents that clearly proclaimed the defeat and condemnation of heresy. The book De gestis Pelagü that we are prefacing belongs to this last genre. But, before dealing with the book, it seems appropriate to collect here the few data that are known about the life of Pelagius, the most fearsome heresiarch with whom the Doctor of Grace had to measure his weapons. The place of birth of Pelagius is unknown and it is only known, from the testimony of his contemporaries, that he was

In this same year we find Pelagius in Carthage, where Saint Augustine saw him once or twice, then very busy with the preparations for the famous conference against the Donatists. From Carthage Pelagius moved to Egypt and shortly after to Palestine, where he was in the year 415 and perhaps before, in 411. Here he seems to have made friends with Saint Jerome; But the friendship did not last long, because the reclusive man from Bethlehem wrote the letter to Ctesiphon in 414, which is a refutation of the doctrines that Pelagius secretly taught his disciples, and the following year three books in the form of dialogue against the Pelagian errors. In the year 415, the synod of Diospolis was held, attended by fourteen bishops of Palestine, to judge Pelagius, accused by the Gallic bishops Heros and Lazarus. The synod condemned the errors attributed to Pelagius and absolved the heresiarch, which gave occasion for Pelagius or his henchmen, anticipating the dissemination of the synod's minutes, to quickly spread a writing throughout the Christian world boasting that Pelagius' doctrine had been approved by fourteen bishops. Upon learning of what had happened in Diospolis, the bishops of proconsular Africa, meeting in Carthage (416), once again condemned the Pelagian errors, along with their authors, Pelagius and Celestius, as long as they did not outright condemn their heresy. The bishops of Numidia, gathered at Milevi, did the same shortly afterwards, and sent the minutes, as did those of proconsular Africa, to Pope Innocent I.

He confirmed the decisions of both councils in letters dated January 27, 417, in which he said that he had received, sent by laymen, the minutes of the synod of Diospolis, but that he did not take them into account because the sincerity of Pelagius was missing in them and because they had been sent to him without being accompanied by any letter from Pelagius or the bishops who had declared him innocent; So he doubted the authenticity of the acts and judged that Pelagius did not believe much in the absolution he propagated, and, therefore, ignoring the acts and based on the report that the African Bishops had sent him, he excommunicated Pelagius and Oelestius as unworthy of ecclesiastical communion. Coming to the specific point of the accusations contained in the accusatory libel, they were read and translated into Greek by means of an interpreter, since the judges did not know Latin. To the charges that the judges made against him, Pelagius responded in Greek. The series of charges and defenses form the background of this book, where the reader can read them summarized in numbers 60-65 of the same. The sentence given by the synod reads as follows: In view of the satisfactory explanations of Pelagius, here present, who professes sound doctrine and condemns and anathematizes doctrine contrary to the faith of the Church, we pronounce that he is worthy of ecclesiastical communion. Such was the synod of Diospolis, which Saint Jerome described as miserable, no doubt considering the scandal that it would cause in the minds of simple people. The causes of this synodal resolution are not difficult to know. Heros and Lazarus did not attend the synod, because one of them was ill. Neither did Orosius nor anyone who accused Pelagius and discovered the meaning of his words, forcing him to expound his doctrine without ambiguities or distortions. Wouldn't the Pelagians be involved in this? Pelagius, then, was absolved and condemned for his heresy or what his lips disapproved, as Saint Augustine says, who did not fail to allege against Pelagius the authority of the Diospolitan synod. Saint himself calls the judges of the synod "pious judges," which sufficiently suggests that Pelagius had surprised their good faith.

PROEMIUS 1. After the minutes of the trial in which fourteen bishops of the province of Palestine reached my hands, venerable bishop Aurelius, they pronounced their sentence declaring Phelagius a Catholic, my hesitations ceased and I resolved to write more prolixly and confidently about the justification with which Pelagius attempted to come clean. It is true that I had already read such justification in a brief writing that he had sent me; But, since no letter was attached to the writing, I feared that my words did not conform to the truth of the episcopal acts, and, therefore, that, if Pelagius perhaps denied having sent me that writing, since it was not easy to convince him otherwise with a single witness, his henchmen would condemn me as an impostor or, at least, as an overly gullible man. As I write now with the minutes in view, I am convinced that your holiness and everyone who reads me will be able to more easily form a complete judgment about my book and say whether Pelagius was able to justify himself or not for the doctrines that were attributed to him.

Let us now say that the holy brothers and bishops of Gaul Heros and Lazarus had presented a memorial against Pelagius; But, it being impossible for them to attend the processing of the process due to the illness of one of them, as we later learned, the charges made against Pelagius were taken from his memorial, the first being having written in one of his books: Only he who has knowledge of the law can live without sin. Having formulated this charge, the synod said: Have you, Pelagius, written this? And he answered: Yes, certainly, but without giving my words the meaning that my adversaries attribute to them. I have not said: He who has knowledge of the law cannot sin, but knowledge of the law is a help not to sin, as it is written: Give them the law as a help. Hearing this answer, the synod said: The doctrine that Pelagius professes is not contrary to the doctrine of the Church. It is true that Pelagius's response is not contrary to the faith of the Church; But the passage cited from his book is. The bishops, since their language was Greek and they had to understand Pelagius' words through the translator, did not want to get involved in disquisitions, paying attention only to the profession of faith that Pelagius made and not stopping to examine the words with which Pelagius expressed his faith. 3. It is one thing that knowledge of the law helps man not to sin, and quite another that he cannot live without sin except someone who has knowledge of the law. We see that the crops are crumbled without the threshing floors on the threshing floor, although the threshing floors, if they are used, serve as a help; that children can go to school without the company of the tutor, although the tutor's help is not useless; that many heal from their ailments without the assistance of the doctor, although the help provided by the doctor is evident; that man can sustain himself with other foods, although he does not use bread, despite the fact that bread is so excellent maintenance. And like these cases, many others could be cited, which easily occur to anyone who reflects a little. It follows from here that there are two ways of help. The first is that without which the thing for which it helps cannot be carried out: thus no one can navigate without a ship, nor speak without words, nor walk without feet, nor see without light, and other things of that nature, such as, for example, that without the grace of God no one can live holy lives.

The other way of help is when we are helped in such a way that, even if we lack help, we can do what we need such help for, as happens in the cases mentioned above: the threshing machine, which helps to break up the crops; of the tutor, who makes the journey to school easier; of artificial medicine, which helps to recover health, and other similar things.

It is important to know to which of these two kinds of aid knowledge of the law belongs. If we say that the knowledge of the law is absolutely necessary to not sin, Pelagius confessed the truth at the trial, and what he wrote in the book is true; But if we say that knowledge of the law is a help, when we have it, to not sin, but we can do without sin even if we lack that knowledge, then we will have to say that1 Pelagius confessed the truth in the trial, thus deserving the approval of the bishops when he said that knowledge of the law helps man not to sin; But what he wrote in his book is not true: That only the man who has knowledge of the law can live without sin, a statement that the judges, because they did not know the Latin language, did not submit to examination, contenting themselves with the explanations of the rapporteur of the case. Which is not surprising, if we take into account that no accuser was present at the trial to force the interpreter to specify the meaning of the words and show how rightly the brothers had been alarmed. Very few have a perfect knowledge of the law. For the multitude of Christ's members, spread throughout the world and unable to attain the knowledge of such a profound and varied law, the piety of a simple faith, the firmest hope in God and sincere charity is sufficient, and, rich with these gifts, they believe that they can be purified from their sins with the grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

This is the fate of the vessels of wrath, which have been made for their condemnation, for even in the condemnation of some God reveals the riches of his glory towards the vessels of mercy. For this reason, after saying: My God, his mercy will prevent me, he added: and will make me look triumphantly on my enemies. This does not happen with the predestined, who are governed by the spirit of God; It is not in vain that they say: Do not allow, Lord, what the wicked desire. Ask God to free you from evil desires by saying: Do not let the pleasures of the belly and sensuality take over me, and do not give me over to lascivious desire. God grants this grace to those who humbly allow themselves to be governed by Him, not to those who believe they are capable of governing themselves and who, very proud of their freedom, refuse to allow themselves to be governed by God. 8. This being so, when the children of God who profess this doctrine and are pleased to be governed and moved3 by the spirit of God, heard or read that Pelagius had written: Everyone is governed by their own will, what great surprise must they not have felt? Pelagius, realizing how bad those words sounded to Catholic ears, answered the questions of the bishops that he had written them because of free will, which, he added, God helps in the choice of good; but when man sins, he is to blame, since he is free. The pious judges accepted this answer as good, without wanting to examine or find out how imprudently those words had been written or what meaning they had in the book; They thought it was enough that Pelagius recognized that God helps free will in the choice of good and that man, when he sins, is responsible for his sin, since free will is enough to sin. Therefore, God rules those whom He helps to choose the good.

ACIAS OF THE PROCESS AGAINST PELAGIO

This judgment must be carried out, which is described in several ways, although the way will be only one. Sometimes the Lord says that he will close the door to those whom he does not admit into his kingdom and that, when they cry and say: Open to us, who ate and drank in your presence, and the rest that they will say, he will answer: I do not know you, workers of iniquity. Other times he says that he will order those who did not want him as king to be brought before him and will order them to be killed in his presence. Other times he says that he will come with great majesty accompanied by his angels so that all the peoples may appear before him and be judged and he will place some on the right, to give them eternal life, the reward of the good works that he will then remember, and others on the left, condemned to eternal fire for lacking good works. Other times he orders that, tied hand and foot, they be thrown into the outer darkness, sometimes the foolish and lazy servant who did not want to negotiate with his Lord's money, sometimes the guest who did not wear the wedding dress at the banquet. Let us also remember how, after the wise virgins enter, he closes the door on the foolish ones. These and other forms of judgment that we do not remember now apply to the future judgment, to which not one or five people, but many, will be subject. Because, if there were not more than one thrown from the banquet into the outer darkness for not wearing the wedding garment, would the Lord not then say: Many are called and few are chosen, since if only one is cast out and condemned, it seems there must have been many left inside. We would go very far if we had to explain each of these words. We will only say now, without prejudice, as they say in money affairs, to a more profound discussion, that the Scriptures declare in various ways that there will be only one mode of judgment, although the rewards and penalties will be diverse due to the diversity of merits. Concretely to the present case, if Pelagius had said that all sinners without exception must be condemned to eternal fire and torture, whoever approved this opinion would condemn himself, because who can boast of being clean of sin?

But since he did not say all or some, but rather used a word with a vague meaning, giving authority to his words with the Gospel, the bishops confirmed the true doctrine; but we are still left without knowing what Pelagius thinks, whose explanation on this matter we have the right to demand even after the sentence pronounced by the bishops.

Scriptures of the law and the prophets, given by God before the advent of Jesus Christ and received by the authority of the Church, are usually designated by the name of the Old Testament. That is why the judges approved Pelagius' response by confessing that all graces had been granted to the Apostle. But there are also other graces outside of these. For although the apostle Saint Paul was such an excellent member of the body of Christ, we are not going to say that the head of this body did not have more abundant and excellent graces, whether in the flesh, or in the soul of the man or creature that the Word of God assumed in unity of person to become our head and make us his body. And in truth, if everyone could have all the graces, it would seem out of purpose to bring up the simile of the members of the body. There are certain things that are common to all members, for example, health, life; but there are others that are specific to each member; from which it results that neither the ear perceives colors nor the eye perceives sounds. The very subscription, "that you serve God," already indicates that this is more the effect of the grace of God than of the will of man, since I do not exhort this, nor command or teach it, but I desire it. What did you intend, then, by quoting my letter in this trial? The last of the accusations was this: That those who repent are not granted forgiveness by the grace and mercy of God, but by the merits and work of those who, through penitence, have become worthy of mercy. The judges acquitted Pelagius because he denied and anathematized these doctrines and the arguments with which he tried to prove them, and said that he had in fact condemned them by reprobing and condemning whatever was contrary to the Catholic faith. Whatever, then, is the way in which Celestius teaches or fails to teach these doctrines, and regardless of what Pelagius has thought or has not thought about them, let us rejoice and give thanks to God and praise Him because the Church has condemned with her judgment such impieties of this newest heresy. 66.

We refrain now from referring to the misdeeds committed with incredible audacity, as is reputed, by a mob of heartless, perverse followers of Pelagius, who took their evil fury to the extreme of persecuting to death the servants of God entrusted to the request of the holy presbyter Jerome, and killed a deacon, and set fire to the monasteries, barely being saved, by the

cordia turris munitior tueretur; tacendum nobis potius video, et expectandum quid illi fratres nostri episcopi de his tantis malis agendum existencement, a quibus eos dissimulare posse, quis credat'? Impia quippe dogmata huiuscemodi hominum, a quibuslibet catholicis, etiam qui ab illis terris longe absunt, redarguenda sunt; ne ubicumque nocere possint, quo pervenire potuerint: impia vero facta, quoruml coeratio ad eipisccipalem pertinet disciplinam, ubi comlmittuntur, ibi potissimum a praesentibus vel in proxima constitutis, diligentia pastorali et pia severitate plectenda sunt. Nos itaque tam longe positi, optere debenmus his causis talem illic finem dari, de quo non sit neoesse ubilibet ulterius iudicare; sed quae nobis potius praedicare conveniat: ut animi omnium, qui illorum scelere fame usquequaque volitante graviter vulnerati sunt, Dei misericordia consequente sanentur. Unde iam huius libri terminus iste sit, qui, ut spero, si sensibus tuis pleasureré meruerit, adiuvante Domino, utilis erit legentibus; tu o quam meo nomine commendatior, et tua diligentia plurimis notior.

Let us wait for our brothers, the bishops, of that region to make their resolutions in view of so many evils, because how are we to suppose that they can conceal them? The impious doctrines of men of this type must be fought by all Catholics, even by those who live far from those countries; But reprehensible crimes, whose punishment falls to the episcopal authority, must be diligently repressed with pious rigor, where they are committed, by the bishops of the place or neighboring places. We, who live so far from the place of those events, long for everything to end without the need for further trials and so that, by the mercy of God, reparation is given to those who suffered such a great scandal with the news of those crimes. And let us put an end to this book, which, if as I hope, is to your liking, with God's favor it will be useful to those who read it, your name, to whom I dedicate it, being a precious recommendation, and your diligence in making it known, a guarantee of its dissemination.
